docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: Debug KBS applications using network visualization, token tracing, fact inspection, and rule execution logging. This guide provides tools and techniques to understand rule behavior and diagnose issues.

docs.title: Debugging Overview
docs.text:
Common debugging scenarios:

  1. Rules not firing - Conditions don't match expected facts
  2. Unexpected rule firing - Rules fire when they shouldn't
  3. Performance issues - Slow rule execution
  4. Incorrect bindings - Variables bound to wrong values
  5. Network structure - Understanding compilation

The examples below print their diagnostics with the debug_me gem (debug_me "message", debug_me { :variable }) where they log events, and with puts where they print a report.

docs.title: Basic Logging
docs.text:
The engine has no debug flag. Subclass it to log fact changes:

require 'kbs'
require 'debug_me'
include DebugMe

class DebugEngine < KBS::Engine
  def add_fact(type, attributes = {})
    fact = super
    # add_fact returns nil when a logically supported fact loses its support
    # before it is added
    debug_me "[FACT ADDED] #{fact.type}: #{fact.attributes.inspect}" if fact
    fact
  end

  def remove_fact(fact)
    debug_me "[FACT REMOVED] #{fact.type}: #{fact.attributes.inspect}"
    super
  end
end

engine = DebugEngine.new

docs.title: Rule Execution Logging
docs.text:
Engine#run pops activations off the agenda and fires each one through fire_activation, so that is the place to record firings. run returns the number of rules fired.

class LoggingEngine < KBS::Engine
  def initialize(**options)
    super
    @rule_log = []
  end

  def fire_activation(activation)
    @rule_log << { rule: activation.rule.name, timestamp: Time.now }
    debug_me "[RULE FIRING] #{activation}"
    super
  end

  def run(limit = nil)
    debug_me "=== Engine Run Started: #{facts.size} facts, #{rules.size} rules, #{agenda.size} activations ==="

    fired = super

    debug_me "=== Engine Run Completed: #{fired} rules fired ==="
    @rule_log.last(fired).each_with_index do |entry, i|
      debug_me "  #{i + 1}. #{entry[:rule]} (#{entry[:timestamp]})"
    end

    fired
  end

  attr_reader :rule_log
end

docs.title: Inspect Current Facts
docs.text:
def inspect_facts(engine)
  puts "\n=== Current Facts ==="

  # Group by type
  facts_by_type = engine.facts.group_by(&:type)

  facts_by_type.each do |type, facts|
    puts "\n#{type} (#{facts.size}):"
    facts.each_with_index do |fact, i|
      puts "  #{i + 1}. #{fact.attributes.inspect}"
      if fact.is_a?(KBS::Blackboard::Fact)
        puts "     UUID: #{fact.uuid}"
      end
    end
  end

  puts "\nTotal facts: #{engine.facts.size}"
end

# Usage
inspect_facts(engine)

A KBS::DSL::KnowledgeBase has print_facts and print_rules built in.

docs.title: Query Fact History (Blackboard)
docs.text:
The blackboard's audit log records every ADD, UPDATE and REMOVE of a fact, newest first.

def inspect_fact_history(engine, fact_uuid)
  return unless engine.is_a?(KBS::Blackboard::Engine)

  puts "\n=== Fact History: #{fact_uuid} ==="

  history = engine.blackboard.get_history(fact_uuid)

  history.each do |entry|
    puts "\n#{entry[:timestamp]}"
    puts "  Action: #{entry[:action]}"
    puts "  Attributes: #{entry[:attributes].inspect}"
  end
end

docs.title: Find Facts by Criteria
docs.text:
def find_facts(engine, **criteria)
  results = engine.facts.select do |fact|
    criteria.all? do |key, value|
      case key
      when :type
        fact.type == value
      else
        fact[key] == value
      end
    end
  end

  puts "\n=== Found #{results.size} facts ==="
  results.each do |fact|
    puts "#{fact.type}: #{fact.attributes.inspect}"
  end

  results
end

# Usage
find_facts(engine, type: :sensor, location: "bedroom")
find_facts(engine, type: :alert, severity: "critical")

docs.title: Built-in Tracing and Inspection
docs.text: The engine can report what it does and how far each rule has matched, without wrapping rules or reading instance variables.

docs.title: watch
docs.text:
watch writes a line for each change to the items you name: :facts, :activations, :rules, or all three when called with no argument. unwatch stops it.

kb = KBS.knowledge_base
kb.rule "paid", priority: 5 do
  on :order, id: :id?
  on :payment, order_id: :id?
  without :hold, order_id: :id?
end

kb.watch
kb.assert(:order, id: 1)
payment = kb.assert(:payment, order_id: 1)
kb.run
kb.retract(payment)

==> fact :order, id: 1
==> fact :payment, order_id: 1
==> Activation 5 paid: fact :order, id: 1; fact :payment, order_id: 1; *
FIRE 1 paid: fact :order, id: 1; fact :payment, order_id: 1; *
<== fact :payment, order_id: 1
Line Meaning ==> fact ... a fact entered working memory <== fact ... a fact left it ==> Activation P rule: ... a match of the rule went on the agenda; P is the rule's priority <== Activation P rule: ... a match was withdrawn before it fired FIRE N rule: ... the rule fired; N counts firings

An activation lists one entry per condition: the matched fact, or * for a without or exists condition.

Lines go to $stdout. Send them elsewhere with engine.trace_output = io; anything that responds to puts works.

docs.title: matches
docs.text:
matches(rule_name) answers "why didn't this rule fire?". For each condition it gives the number of facts that fit the condition on its own (alpha_matches) and the number of partial matches of the rule up to and including it (partial_matches).

kb.assert(:order, id: 2)
kb.matches("paid")
# => {rule: "paid",
#     conditions:
#      [{keyword: "on", type: :order, alpha_matches: 2, partial_matches: 2},
#       {keyword: "on", type: :payment, alpha_matches: 0, partial_matches: 0},
#       {keyword: "without", type: :hold, alpha_matches: 0, partial_matches: 0}],
#     matches: 0,
#     activations: 0}

Read down the list: the first condition with partial_matches: 0 is the one that stops the rule. Here two orders match, and no payment does. When alpha_matches is positive and partial_matches is zero, facts fit the pattern but a shared variable does not line up with the earlier conditions.

matches: counts complete matches, and activations: the ones that have not fired yet.

docs.title: join_activity
docs.text:
engine.join_activity(rule_name) shows what each condition has cost since the engine started, or since engine.reset_join_activity.

kb.engine.join_activity("paid")[1]
# => {keyword: "on", type: :payment, indexed: true,
#     left_activations: 2, right_activations: 1, comparisons: 1, matches: 1}
Key Meaning indexed the condition is joined through a hash index on a shared variable left_activations partial matches that arrived from the conditions before it right_activations facts that arrived for this condition comparisons candidates looked at matches candidates that passed

A condition with comparisons far above matches is doing wasted work: it has no shared variable to index on, or its pattern is too loose. Move a more selective condition ahead of it. Rules that share a node report the same counts for it.

docs.title: network_stats
docs.text:
kb.engine.network_stats
# => {rules: 1, facts: 2, alpha_memories: 3, beta_nodes: 3, conditions: 3,
#     partial_matches: 2, activations: 0}

beta_nodes below conditions means rules are sharing joins. A partial_matches count that grows much faster than facts points at a join without a shared variable.

docs.title: Trace Rule Execution
docs.text:
engine.rules lists the rules, and Rule#action can be replaced. An action that takes two arguments receives the matched facts and the variable bindings.

class RuleTracer
  def initialize(engine)
    @engine = engine
    @traces = []
  end

  def wrap_rules
    @engine.rules.each do |rule|
      wrap_rule(rule)
    end
  end

  def wrap_rule(rule)
    original_action = rule.action

    rule.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
      trace = {
        rule: rule.name,
        timestamp: Time.now,
        facts: facts.map { |f| { type: f.type, attrs: f.attributes } },
        bindings: bindings.dup
      }

      debug_me "[RULE FIRING] #{rule.name}"
      debug_me "  Facts: #{facts.map(&:type).join(', ')}"
      debug_me "  Bindings: #{bindings.inspect}"

      result = original_action&.call(facts, bindings)

      trace[:duration] = (Time.now - trace[:timestamp])
      @traces << trace

      debug_me "  Duration: #{trace[:duration]}s"

      result
    end
  end

  attr_reader :traces
end

# Usage
tracer = RuleTracer.new(engine)
tracer.wrap_rules
engine.run
debug_me "Total rule firings: #{tracer.traces.size}"

docs.title: Test Individual Conditions
docs.text:
A condition's pattern holds only the attribute tests; its fact type is condition.type. A helper that checks one fact against one condition, the way the alpha network does, makes the other tools below simple. Predicates such as greater_than(25) are Procs inside the pattern and are called by the match.

# Whether `fact` fits `condition` on its own, ignoring the joins on
# ?variables shared with other conditions.
def condition_matches?(fact, condition)
  fact.type == condition.type &&
    condition.pattern.all? do |key, expected|
      KBS::PatternMatching.value_matches?(fact[key], expected)
    end
end

def test_condition(engine, condition)
  puts "\n=== Testing Condition ==="
  puts "Type: #{condition.type}"
  puts "Pattern: #{condition.pattern.inspect}"

  # Find matching facts
  matches = engine.facts.select { |fact| condition_matches?(fact, condition) }

  puts "\nMatching facts: #{matches.size}"
  matches.each do |fact|
    puts "  #{fact.attributes.inspect}"
    puts "  Bindings: #{condition.bindings_from(fact).inspect}"
  end

  matches
end

# Usage
condition = KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, {
  type: "temperature",
  value: ->(v) { v > 25 }
})

test_condition(engine, condition)

docs.title: Why Did Rule Fire?
docs.text:
Each rule ends in a production node, engine.production_nodes[rule_name], that holds the rule's current complete matches as tokens. A token knows its facts and whether it has fired.

def why_rule_fired(engine, rule_name)
  node = engine.production_nodes[rule_name]

  return unless node

  puts "\n=== Why '#{rule_name}' Fired ==="

  node.tokens.each_with_index do |token, i|
    puts "\nMatch #{i + 1} (#{token.fired? ? 'fired' : 'waiting on the agenda'}):"
    token.facts.each do |fact|
      puts "    - #{fact.type}: #{fact.attributes.inspect}"
    end
    puts "  Bindings: #{node.rule.bindings_for(token.facts).inspect}"
  end
end

docs.title: Why Didn't Rule Fire?
docs.text:
This checks each condition on its own with condition_matches?, so a without condition is reported as blocked by any fact that fits it, even one whose ?variables differ from the facts matched before it.

def why_rule_didnt_fire(engine, rule_name)
  rule = engine.rules.find { |r| r.name == rule_name }

  return unless rule

  puts "\n=== Why '#{rule_name}' Didn't Fire ==="

  # Check each condition
  failing_condition = nil

  rule.conditions.each_with_index do |condition, i|
    puts "\nCondition #{i + 1}: #{condition.summary}"

    matches = engine.facts.select { |f| condition_matches?(f, condition) }

    if condition.negated
      puts "  Negated condition"
      if matches.empty?
        puts "  ✓ PASSED (no matching facts)"
      else
        puts "  ✗ FAILED (#{matches.size} matching facts found, but should be absent)"
        failing_condition = i
        matches.each do |fact|
          puts "    Blocking fact: #{fact.attributes.inspect}"
        end
      end
    elsif matches.empty?
      puts "  ✗ FAILED (no matching facts)"
      failing_condition = i

      # Suggest similar facts
      similar = engine.facts.select { |f| f.type == condition.type }
      if similar.any?
        puts "  Similar facts (#{similar.size}):"
        similar.first(3).each do |fact|
          puts "    - #{fact.attributes.inspect}"
        end
      end
    else
      puts "  ✓ PASSED (#{matches.size} facts)"
    end

    break if failing_condition
  end

  if failing_condition
    puts "\n⚠️  Rule failed at condition #{failing_condition + 1}"
  else
    puts <<~MSG

      ✓ Every condition has matching facts on its own. If the rule still
        has not fired, check that ?variables shared between conditions hold
        equal values, and whether it already fired for these facts: an
        activation fires once (see why_rule_fired).
    MSG
  end
end

# Usage
why_rule_didnt_fire(engine, "detect_high_temperature")

docs.title: Inspect the Agenda
docs.text:
Matches wait on the agenda until engine.run fires them. engine.agenda.to_a lists the pending activations in firing order; each prints as its priority, rule name and facts.

def inspect_agenda(engine)
  puts "\n=== Agenda (#{engine.agenda.size} pending, strategy: #{engine.strategy}) ==="
  engine.agenda.to_a.each_with_index do |activation, i|
    puts "  #{i + 1}. #{activation}"
  end
end

docs.title: Logical Support
docs.text:
A fact asserted by a rule with logical conditions is retracted when the match of those conditions goes away. To see why such a fact exists, or why it vanished:

engine.logically_supported?(fact)  # asserted under logical conditions?
engine.dependencies(fact)          # the matches supporting it, each an array of facts
engine.dependents(fact)            # facts that lose a support if this one is retracted

docs.title: Print Network Structure
docs.text:
engine.alpha_memories maps each condition pattern (with its fact type under :type) to the alpha memory that holds the facts fitting it.

def visualize_network(engine)
  puts "\n=== RETE Network Structure ==="

  # Alpha network
  puts "\nALPHA NETWORK:"
  engine.alpha_memories.each do |pattern, memory|
    puts "  #{pattern.inspect}"
    puts "    Items: #{memory.items.size}"
  end

  # Production nodes
  puts "\nPRODUCTION NODES:"
  engine.production_nodes.each do |name, node|
    puts "  #{name}: #{node.tokens.size} matches"
  end

  puts "\nSTATISTICS:"
  puts "  Alpha memories: #{engine.alpha_memories.size}"
  puts "  Total facts: #{engine.facts.size}"
  puts "  Rules: #{engine.rules.size}"
  puts "  Pending activations: #{engine.agenda.size}"
end

docs.title: Graphviz Export
docs.text:
def export_to_graphviz(engine, filename = "network.dot")
  File.open(filename, 'w') do |f|
    f.puts "digraph RETE {"
    f.puts "  rankdir=TB;"
    f.puts "  node [shape=box];"

    # Alpha nodes
    f.puts "\n  // Alpha Network"
    engine.alpha_memories.each_with_index do |(pattern, memory), i|
      node_id = "alpha_#{i}"
      label = "#{pattern[:type]}\\n#{memory.items.size} facts"
      f.puts "  #{node_id} [label=\"#{label}\", style=filled, fillcolor=lightblue];"
    end

    # Production nodes
    f.puts "\n  // Production Nodes"
    engine.rules.each_with_index do |rule, i|
      node_id = "rule_#{i}"
      label = "#{rule.name}\\n#{rule.priority}"
      f.puts "  #{node_id} [label=\"#{label}\", style=filled, fillcolor=lightgreen];"
    end

    # Edges (simplified)
    # ...

    f.puts "}"
  end

  puts "Network exported to #{filename}"
  puts "Render with: dot -Tpng #{filename} -o network.png"
end

# Usage
export_to_graphviz(engine)

docs.title: Trace Token Propagation
docs.text:
An alpha memory receives a new fact through activate(fact) and passes it on to its join nodes through right_activate(fact).

class TokenTracer
  def initialize
    @trace = []
  end

  def log_activation(node_type, node_id, token)
    @trace << {
      timestamp: Time.now,
      node_type: node_type,
      node_id: node_id,
      token: token.inspect
    }

    debug_me "[#{node_type}] #{node_id}: #{token.inspect}"
  end

  def print_trace
    puts "\n=== Token Trace ==="
    @trace.each_with_index do |entry, i|
      puts "\n#{i + 1}. [#{entry[:node_type]}] #{entry[:node_id]}"
      puts "   Time: #{entry[:timestamp]}"
      puts "   Token: #{entry[:token]}"
    end
  end

  attr_reader :trace
end

# Usage: Instrument nodes
tracer = TokenTracer.new

# Wrap alpha activation
engine.alpha_memories.each_value do |alpha_memory|
  alpha_memory.define_singleton_method(:activate) do |fact|
    tracer.log_activation("AlphaMemory", object_id, fact)
    super(fact)
  end
end

docs.title: Debug Console
docs.text:
class DebugConsole
  def initialize(engine)
    @engine = engine
  end

  def start
    loop do
      print "\nkbs> "
      input = gets&.chomp

      break if input.nil? || input == "exit"

      case input
      when "facts"
        inspect_facts(@engine)
      when "rules"
        list_rules
      when "run"
        fired = @engine.run
        puts "Engine ran successfully (#{fired} rules fired)"
      when /^add (\w+) (.+)$/
        type = $1.to_sym
        attrs = eval($2)  # UNSAFE: eval user input (for demo only)
        @engine.add_fact(type, attrs)
        puts "Fact added"
      when /^remove (\d+)$/
        fact = @engine.facts[$1.to_i]
        @engine.remove_fact(fact) if fact
        puts "Fact removed"
      when /^why (.+)$/
        why_rule_didnt_fire(@engine, $1)
      when "help"
        print_help
      else
        puts "Unknown command: #{input}"
        print_help
      end
    end
  end

  def list_rules
    puts "\n=== Rules ==="
    @engine.rules.each_with_index do |rule, i|
      puts "#{i}. #{rule.name} (priority: #{rule.priority}, conditions: #{rule.conditions.size})"
    end
  end

  def print_help
    puts <<~HELP

      Commands:
        facts              - List all facts
        rules              - List all rules
        run                - Run engine
        add TYPE {ATTRS}   - Add fact
        remove INDEX       - Remove fact
        why RULE_NAME      - Explain why rule didn't fire
        exit               - Exit console
        help               - Show this help

    HELP
  end
end

# Usage
console = DebugConsole.new(engine)
console.start

docs.title: Step-Through Debugger
docs.text:
The debugger wraps every rule's action when it is created. It stops at the rules with a breakpoint, or at every rule in step mode.

class StepDebugger
  def initialize(engine)
    @engine = engine
    @breakpoints = []
    @step_mode = false

    @engine.rules.each do |rule|
      wrap_rule_with_breakpoint(rule)
    end
  end

  def add_breakpoint(rule_name)
    @breakpoints << rule_name
    puts "Breakpoint added: #{rule_name}"
  end

  def enable_step_mode
    @step_mode = true
  end

  def wrap_rule_with_breakpoint(rule)
    original_action = rule.action

    rule.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
      if @breakpoints.include?(rule.name) || @step_mode
        puts "\n🔴 BREAKPOINT: #{rule.name}"
        puts "Facts: #{facts.map { |f| { type: f.type, attrs: f.attributes } }}"
        puts "Bindings: #{bindings.inspect}"

        print "Continue? [y/n/i(nspect)] "
        response = gets.to_s.chomp

        case response
        when 'n'
          puts "Skipping rule"
          return
        when 'i'
          inspect_rule_context(facts, bindings)
        end
      end

      original_action&.call(facts, bindings)
    end
  end

  def inspect_rule_context(facts, bindings)
    puts "\n=== Rule Context ==="
    puts "Facts (#{facts.size}):"
    facts.each_with_index do |fact, i|
      puts "  #{i}. #{fact.type}: #{fact.attributes.inspect}"
    end

    puts "\nBindings:"
    bindings.each do |var, value|
      puts "  #{var} => #{value.inspect}"
    end

    print "\nPress Enter to continue..."
    gets
  end
end

# Usage
debugger = StepDebugger.new(engine)
debugger.add_breakpoint("high_temperature_alert")
# debugger.enable_step_mode  # stop at every rule
engine.run

docs.title: Verify Pattern Matching
docs.text:
Fact#matches? takes a pattern whose :type key, if present, is the fact type. A Proc in the pattern is called with the attribute's value, and a ?variable matches any value.

def verify_pattern_match(fact, pattern)
  puts "\n=== Pattern Match Verification ==="
  puts "Fact: #{fact.attributes.inspect}"
  puts "Pattern: #{pattern.inspect}"

  result = fact.matches?(pattern)
  puts "Result: #{result}"

  # Detail each attribute
  pattern.each do |key, expected|
    next if key == :type

    actual = fact[key]
    match = KBS::PatternMatching.value_matches?(actual, expected)

    puts "\n  #{key}:"
    puts "    Expected: #{expected.inspect}"
    puts "    Actual: #{actual.inspect}"
    puts "    Match: #{match ? '✓' : '✗'}"
  end

  result
end

docs.title: Diagnose Join Issues
docs.text:
def diagnose_join(engine, condition1, condition2)
  puts "\n=== Join Diagnosis ==="

  # Find matches for each condition
  matches1 = engine.facts.select { |f| condition_matches?(f, condition1) }
  matches2 = engine.facts.select { |f| condition_matches?(f, condition2) }

  puts "\nCondition 1 matches: #{matches1.size}"
  matches1.first(3).each { |f| puts "  - #{f.attributes.inspect}" }

  puts "\nCondition 2 matches: #{matches2.size}"
  matches2.first(3).each { |f| puts "  - #{f.attributes.inspect}" }

  # Find join variables
  join_vars = condition1.variable_bindings.keys & condition2.variable_bindings.keys

  puts "\nJoin variables: #{join_vars.inspect}"

  if join_vars.empty?
    puts "⚠️  No shared variables - conditions are independent"
  else
    # Check if any combinations match
    combinations = 0
    matches1.each do |f1|
      matches2.each do |f2|
        # Extract bindings
        bindings1 = condition1.bindings_from(f1)
        bindings2 = condition2.bindings_from(f2)

        # Check join
        if join_vars.all? { |v| bindings1[v] == bindings2[v] }
          combinations += 1
        end
      end
    end

    puts "Valid combinations: #{combinations}"
  end
end

docs.title: Track Memory Usage
docs.text:
require 'objspace'

def track_memory_usage(engine)
  puts "\n=== Memory Usage ==="

  # Facts
  fact_size = engine.facts.sum { |f| ObjectSpace.memsize_of(f) }
  puts "Facts: #{(fact_size / 1024.0).round(2)} KB (#{engine.facts.size} facts)"

  # Alpha memories
  alpha_size = 0
  engine.alpha_memories.each_value do |memory|
    alpha_size += ObjectSpace.memsize_of(memory)
    alpha_size += memory.items.sum { |f| ObjectSpace.memsize_of(f) }
  end
  puts "Alpha network: #{(alpha_size / 1024.0).round(2)} KB"

  total = fact_size + alpha_size
  puts "\nTotal: #{(total / 1024.0).round(2)} KB"
end

docs.title: Debugging Checklist
docs.text:
• Verify facts are added with correct types and attributes
  • Check condition patterns match fact structure
  • Test predicates independently
  • Ensure variables are bound correctly across conditions
  • Check negated conditions for blocking facts
  • Verify rule priorities and the agenda's strategy
  • Inspect the agenda for pending activations
  • Inspect network structure
  • Trace rule execution
  • Monitor memory usage
  • Check for infinite loops (engine.run(limit) stops after limit firings)

docs.title: Performance Tuning
docs.text: Optimize KBS applications for speed, scalability, and efficiency. This guide covers profiling, benchmarking, rule optimization, and storage backend selection.

docs.title: Performance Overview
docs.text:
KBS performance depends on:

  1. Rule Complexity - Number of conditions, predicates, and joins
  2. Fact Volume - Size of working memory
  3. Network Structure - Shared nodes and network branching
  4. Storage Backend - SQLite, Redis, or in-memory
  5. Action Efficiency - Time spent in rule actions

docs.title: RETE Regex Baseline
docs.text:
The current regex path uses Ruby's built-in Regexp#match? inside a condition predicate, which Fact#matches? evaluates while facts are asserted. Run the reproducible benchmark from the repository root:

ruby -Ilib benchmarks/regex_baseline.rb

It compares regex matching with an equivalent String#start_with? predicate both directly and during RETE fact assertion. ITERATIONS and REPEATS environment variables can adjust the workload.

Baseline recorded on Ruby 3.2.3, x86_64-linux-gnu (20,000 values per sample, five samples; median elapsed time; 50% matching values):

Measurement Throughput Direct Regexp#match? 7,448,440 comparisons/sec Direct String#start_with? 14,964,594 comparisons/sec RETE regex predicate 415,008 facts/sec RETE prefix predicate 482,253 facts/sec

The direct measurements isolate predicate cost; RETE measurements also include fact creation and network propagation, so compare those rows only with each other. These are environment-specific baseline observations, not performance targets. Re-run the benchmark on the target Ruby/runtime before evaluating a regex engine change.

docs.title: RETE Scaling
docs.text:
benchmarks/rete_scaling.rb measures how the network scales as facts and rules are added: a two-condition join on a shared variable, the same join negated, firing the matches with run, retraction, and fact assertion against many alpha memories.

ruby -Ilib benchmarks/rete_scaling.rb
SIZES=500,1000,2000 REPEATS=5 ruby -Ilib benchmarks/rete_scaling.rb

A scenario that scales linearly keeps its rate as the size grows.

In the tables below, the "scan" columns were recorded before the indexing and linking changes; the script measures only the current code, so a re-run reproduces the right-hand columns.

Joins on a shared ?variable are hash joins. The alpha memory is indexed on the fact's fields and the beta memory on the token's fields, so a new fact or token only visits the entries that share its value. Recorded on Ruby 4.0.9, arm64-darwin (median of 3), for n orders joined with n payments on ?id:

n Memory scan Hash index 500 15,294 facts/sec 313,873 facts/sec 1000 7,949 facts/sec 327,279 facts/sec 2000 4,120 facts/sec 360,101 facts/sec

Retraction follows links instead of searching. The engine records which alpha memories each fact went into, each join records the tokens it built from each fact, and each token records its children, so removing a fact touches only its own matches. Removing n joined payments:

n Memory scan Linked 500 16,576 facts/sec 500,500 facts/sec 1000 8,566 facts/sec 392,311 facts/sec 2000 4,251 facts/sec 484,848 facts/sec

Asserting a fact does not test it against every pattern. Alpha memories are grouped by fact type, and those that test an attribute against a constant are hashed on that value, so the cost does not grow with the number of rules. 2000 asserts against n rules:

n Each on its own type, scan Indexed Each on its own constant, scan Indexed 500 32,965 facts/sec 292,912 facts/sec 7,877 facts/sec 315,657 facts/sec 1000 17,316 facts/sec 336,361 facts/sec 3,960 facts/sec 300,661 facts/sec 2000 8,770 facts/sec 321,492 facts/sec 1,996 facts/sec 310,029 facts/sec

A pattern is hashed on its first attribute compared with a plain value. A pattern that only uses predicates or variables is tested for every fact of its type, so put a constant test in the pattern when the rule has one.

without and exists conditions link each partial match to the facts that satisfy it, and each fact to the matches it affects. Retracting n payments that each block one order in a without:

n Memory scan Linked 500 21,668 facts/sec 302,847 facts/sec 1000 10,445 facts/sec 235,405 facts/sec 2000 4,915 facts/sec 244,439 facts/sec

Rules that start with the same conditions share the nodes for them. 50 rules that each begin with the same join of n orders and n payments:

n A join per rule Shared join 500 8,200 facts/sec 105,541 facts/sec 1000 9,633 facts/sec 118,842 facts/sec 2000 7,740 facts/sec 107,411 facts/sec

Write the conditions rules have in common first, in the same order and with the same variable names: a pattern includes its variable names, so id: :id? and id: :order_id? are different patterns.

Only equality between two conditions is indexed. A condition with no shared variable, or one that only uses predicates, still scans its memories, so put a shared variable on the join where the data allows it.

Firing does not sort the agenda. As in CLIPS, activations are grouped by salience, and under the :definition strategy also by rule; within a group, :depth takes the newest first and the other strategies the oldest first, so adding and popping an activation compare nothing. Three rules at different priorities on the same join of n orders and n payments, asserted and then run (3n firings, :definition strategy):

n 0.3.0 (binary heap) 0.4.0 (salience groups, fewer allocations) 0.3.0, YJIT 0.4.0, YJIT 500 110,726 firings/sec 346,420 firings/sec 140,845 firings/sec 750,375 firings/sec 1000 108,980 firings/sec 368,415 firings/sec 175,757 firings/sec 853,728 firings/sec 2000 97,575 firings/sec 360,382 firings/sec 152,858 firings/sec 835,073 firings/sec

docs.title: Running with YJIT
docs.text:
YJIT, the JIT compiler built into CRuby, speeds up KBS by roughly 1.5 to 2.5 times on these benchmarks with no code changes. Turn it on with any of:

ruby --yjit app.rb            # one process
RUBY_YJIT_ENABLE=1 ruby app.rb  # through the environment, e.g. in a Procfile

RubyVM::YJIT.enable           # from code, early in boot
RubyVM::YJIT.enabled?         # => true

Compare both ways on your own rules by running the benchmark with and without the flag:

ruby -Ilib benchmarks/rete_scaling.rb
ruby --yjit -Ilib benchmarks/rete_scaling.rb

docs.title: Basic Benchmark
docs.text:
require 'benchmark'
require 'kbs'

kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "simple_rule" do
    on :fact, value: :v?
    perform do |facts, bindings|
      # Simple action
    end
  end
end

# Benchmark fact addition
time = Benchmark.measure do
  10_000.times do |i|
    kb.fact :fact, value: i
  end
end

puts "Added 10,000 facts in #{time.real} seconds"
puts "#{(10_000 / time.real).round(2)} facts/second"

# Benchmark engine run

  kb.run
end

puts "Ran engine in #{time.real} seconds"

docs.title: Comprehensive Benchmark
docs.text:
require 'benchmark'
require 'kbs/blackboard'

class KBSBenchmark
  def initialize(engine_type: :memory)
    @engine_type = engine_type
    @results = {}
  end

  # A fresh engine of the type under test
  def new_engine
    case @engine_type
    when :memory
      KBS::Engine.new
    when :blackboard_sqlite
      KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: ':memory:')
    when :blackboard_redis
      store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(
        url: 'redis://localhost:6379/15'  # Test database
      )
      KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(store: store)
    end
  end

  def benchmark_fact_addition(count: 10_000)
    kb = KBS.knowledge_base(engine: new_engine)

    time = Benchmark.measure do
      count.times do |i|
        kb.fact :fact, id: i, value: rand(1000)
      end
    end

    @results[:fact_addition] = {
      count: count,
      time: time.real,
      rate: (count / time.real).round(2)
    }
  end

  def benchmark_simple_rules(fact_count: 1000, rule_count: 10)
    kb = KBS.knowledge_base(engine: new_engine) do
      # Add rules
      rule_count.times do |i|
        rule "rule_#{i}" do
          on :fact, value: :v?
          perform { }  # Minimal action
        end
      end

      # Add facts
      fact_count.times do |i|
        fact :fact, value: i
      end
    end

    # Benchmark engine run
    time = Benchmark.measure do
      kb.run
    end

    @results[:simple_rules] = {
      fact_count: fact_count,
      rule_count: rule_count,
      time: time.real
    }
  end

  def benchmark_complex_joins(fact_count: 500)
    kb = KBS.knowledge_base(engine: new_engine) do
      # Rule with 3-way join
      rule "complex_join" do
        on :a, id: :id?, value: :v?
        on :b, a_id: :id?, score: :s?
        on :c, b_score: :s?
        perform do |facts, bindings|
          # Action
        end
      end

      # Add facts
      fact_count.times do |i|
        fact :a, id: i, value: rand(100)
        fact :b, a_id: i, score: rand(100)
        fact :c, b_score: i
      end
    end

    # Benchmark
    time = Benchmark.measure do
      kb.run
    end

    @results[:complex_joins] = {
      fact_count: fact_count * 3,
      time: time.real
    }
  end

  def benchmark_negation(fact_count: 1000)
    kb = KBS.knowledge_base(engine: new_engine) do
      # Rule with negation
      rule "negation_rule" do
        on :positive, id: :id?
        without :negative, id: :id?
        perform do |facts, bindings|
          # Action
        end
      end

      # Add facts (50% will match)
      fact_count.times do |i|
        fact :positive, id: i
        fact :negative, id: i if i.even?
      end
    end

    # Benchmark
    time = Benchmark.measure do
      kb.run
    end

    @results[:negation] = {
      fact_count: fact_count + (fact_count / 2),
      time: time.real
    }
  end

  def run_all
    puts "=== KBS Performance Benchmark (#{@engine_type}) ==="

    benchmark_fact_addition
    puts "\nFact Addition:"
    puts "  #{@results[:fact_addition][:count]} facts in #{@results[:fact_addition][:time].round(4)}s"
    puts "  Rate: #{@results[:fact_addition][:rate]} facts/sec"

    benchmark_simple_rules
    puts "\nSimple Rules:"
    puts "  #{@results[:simple_rules][:rule_count]} rules, #{@results[:simple_rules][:fact_count]} facts"
    puts "  Time: #{@results[:simple_rules][:time].round(4)}s"

    benchmark_complex_joins
    puts "\nComplex Joins (3-way):"
    puts "  #{@results[:complex_joins][:fact_count]} facts"
    puts "  Time: #{@results[:complex_joins][:time].round(4)}s"

    benchmark_negation
    puts "\nNegation:"
    puts "  #{@results[:negation][:fact_count]} facts"
    puts "  Time: #{@results[:negation][:time].round(4)}s"

    @results
  end
end

# Run benchmarks
memory_bench = KBSBenchmark.new(engine_type: :memory)
memory_results = memory_bench.run_all

# Compare with blackboard
blackboard_bench = KBSBenchmark.new(engine_type: :blackboard_sqlite)
blackboard_results = blackboard_bench.run_all

# Compare
puts "\n=== Performance Comparison ==="
puts "Fact addition: Memory is #{(blackboard_results[:fact_addition][:time] / memory_results[:fact_addition][:time]).round(2)}x faster"

Run it with ruby -Ilib, as for the scripts in benchmarks/: on Ruby 4, benchmark is a bundled gem that is not in the project's Gemfile, so bundle exec cannot load it.

docs.title: Condition Ordering
docs.text:
Order conditions from most to least selective:

# Bad: Generic condition first
KBS::Rule.new("inefficient") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:any_event, { error_id: :id? }),  # Matches ALL events (large alpha memory)
    KBS::Condition.new(:critical_error, { id: :id?, severity: "critical" })  # Selective
  ]
end

# Good: Selective condition first
KBS::Rule.new("efficient") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:critical_error, { id: :id?, severity: "critical" }),  # Selective
    KBS::Condition.new(:any_event, { error_id: :id? })  # Filtered by join on ?id
  ]
end

Why it matters:

Bad ordering:
  any_event alpha: 10,000 facts
  Join produces 10,000 tokens
  critical_error alpha: 5 facts
  Join filters down to 5 final matches
  → 10,000 token propagations

Good ordering:
  critical_error alpha: 5 facts
  Join produces 5 tokens
  any_event alpha: 10,000 facts
  Join filters to 5 final matches
  → 5 token propagations (2000x fewer!)

Both orderings find the 5 matches through a hash lookup on ?id; the difference is the 10,000 partial-match tokens the bad ordering builds and stores in its first beta memory.

docs.title: Predicate Efficiency
docs.text:
Use simple predicates. A predicate is a Proc given as an attribute's expected value; it is called with that attribute's value for each candidate fact as it is asserted:

# Bad: Complex predicate
KBS::Condition.new(:data, { raw_data: lambda { |raw|
  # Expensive operations
  json = JSON.parse(raw)
  result = ComplexCalculation.new(json).process
  result > threshold
} })

# Good: Pre-process data
engine.add_fact(:data, {
  value: calculate_value(raw_data),  # Pre-calculated
  processed: true
})

KBS::Condition.new(:data, { value: ->(v) { v > threshold } })  # Simple comparison

docs.title: Network Sharing
docs.text:
Leverage shared alpha memories (join nodes and beta memories are built per rule and are not shared). Two conditions share an alpha memory only when their type and whole pattern are equal, variable names included:

rule1 = KBS::Rule.new("rule1") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { kind: "temperature", value: :v? })
  ]
end

rule2 = KBS::Rule.new("rule2") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { kind: "temperature", value: :v? })  # SAME pattern
  ]
end

# Engine automatically shares alpha memory for :sensor + kind="temperature"
# Adding 1 temperature sensor fact activates BOTH rules efficiently.
# With value: :v1? in one rule and :v2? in the other, the patterns differ
# and each rule gets its own alpha memory.

Sharing visualization:

Facts → AlphaMemory(:sensor, type=temperature) ──┬─→ Rule1
                                                  └─→ Rule2

Instead of:
Facts → AlphaMemory1(:sensor) → Rule1
     └→ AlphaMemory2(:sensor) → Rule2  (duplicate work)

docs.title: Minimize Negations
docs.text:
Negations cost more than a plain join: each keeps links between partial matches and the facts that block them, and a negation without a shared ?variable checks the whole alpha memory for every new token:

# Expensive: Multiple negations
KBS::Rule.new("many_negations") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:a, {}),
    KBS::Condition.new(:b, {}, negated: true),
    KBS::Condition.new(:c, {}, negated: true),
    KBS::Condition.new(:d, {}, negated: true)
  ]
end
# Each of these negations has no shared variable, so it checks its whole
# alpha memory for every token

# Better: Use positive logic
engine.add_fact(:conditions_clear, {}) unless b_exists? || c_exists? || d_exists?

KBS::Rule.new("positive_logic") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:a, {}),
    KBS::Condition.new(:conditions_clear, {})
  ]
end

docs.title: Batch Operations
docs.text:
Group related operations:

# Add facts one by one with run after each
1000.times do |i|
  engine.add_fact(:item, { id: i })
  engine.run  # Run engine 1000 times
end

# Batch add, then run once
1000.times do |i|
  engine.add_fact(:item, { id: i })
end
engine.run  # Run engine once

Matching happens as each fact is added, and run only pops the agenda, so both forms do about the same matching work. The difference is when rules fire: running after each fact fires rules before later facts arrive, while one run lets priorities and the strategy order all activations together, and lets a later fact cancel an activation before it fires. With a blackboard, wrap the batch in memory.transaction to commit once.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
require 'benchmark'

# In-memory (fastest)
memory_engine = KBS::Engine.new

# SQLite (persistent, slower)
sqlite_engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'test.db')

# Redis (persistent, fast)
require 'kbs/blackboard/persistence/redis_store'
redis_store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(
  url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0'
)
redis_engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(store: redis_store)

# Benchmark
engines = {
  memory: memory_engine,
  sqlite: sqlite_engine,
  redis: redis_engine
}

engines.each do |name, engine|
  time = Benchmark.measure do
    10_000.times { |i| engine.add_fact(:test, { value: i }) }
  end

  puts "#{name}: #{(10_000 / time.real).round(2)} facts/sec"
end

# One run on Ruby 4.0.9, arm64-darwin, file-backed SQLite, local Redis:
# memory: ~930,000 facts/sec
# sqlite: ~1,900 facts/sec
# redis:  ~1,700 facts/sec

Each blackboard add_fact writes the fact and an audit entry; outside a transaction SQLite commits each one, and Redis makes several round trips. Measure on your own hardware and network.

docs.title: Backend Decision Matrix
docs.text:
In-Memory (KBS::Engine): - ✅ Fastest (no I/O) - ✅ Simple (no setup) - ❌ No persistence - Use when: Prototyping, short-lived processes, pure computation

SQLite (KBS::Blackboard::Engine): - ✅ Persistent - ✅ ACID transactions - ✅ No dependencies - ❌ Slower writes (each fact also writes an audit entry; batch in a transaction) - Use when: Single process, moderate load, need durability

Redis (RedisStore): - ✅ Shared between processes - ✅ In-memory storage - ❌ Requires Redis server - ❌ A network round trip per operation; not faster than SQLite per fact in the run above - Use when: High throughput, multiple processes, real-time systems

Hybrid (HybridStore): - ✅ Fast (Redis) + durable (SQLite) - ❌ Most complex - Use when: Production, need both speed and audit trail

docs.title: SQLite Optimization
docs.text:
Blackboard::Engine.new takes only db_path:, store:, strategy: and fact_duplication:. Set SQLite pragmas on the store's database handle:

engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'optimized.db')
db = engine.blackboard.store.db   # SQLite3::Database

db.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")      # Write-Ahead Logging (better concurrency)
db.execute("PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL")    # Balance safety/speed
db.execute("PRAGMA cache_size = -64000")     # 64MB cache
db.busy_timeout = 5000                       # Wait 5s for locks

Batching writes in engine.blackboard.transaction { ... } usually matters more: in one run, 1,000 add_fact calls took 0.6 s one by one and 0.02 s in a single transaction.

docs.title: Redis Optimization
docs.text:
RedisStore.new takes url:, session_id: and redis:. To configure the connection (timeouts, reconnects), build the Redis client yourself and pass it in; the store has no connection pool:

redis = Redis.new(url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0', reconnect_attempts: 3)
store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(redis: redis)

engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(store: store)

# Enable Redis persistence (optional)
# In redis.conf:
#   save 900 1
#   appendonly yes

docs.title: Custom Instrumentation
docs.text:
class InstrumentedEngine < KBS::Engine
  def initialize
    super
    @metrics = {
      fact_additions: 0,
      rule_firings: 0,
      alpha_activations: 0,
      beta_activations: 0
    }
  end

  def add_fact(type, attributes = {})
    @metrics[:fact_additions] += 1
    super
  end

  def fire_activation(activation)
    @metrics[:rule_firings] += 1
    super
  end

  def run(limit = nil)
    start = Time.now
    result = super
    elapsed = Time.now - start

    puts "Engine run: #{elapsed}s"
    puts "  Facts: #{facts.size}"
    puts "  Rules fired: #{@metrics[:rule_firings]}"

    result
  end

  def report_metrics
    @metrics
  end
end

docs.title: 1. Large Alpha Memories
docs.text:
Problem: Conditions matching many facts slow down joins

# Slow: Matches ALL events
KBS::Condition.new(:event, {})  # Alpha memory: 100,000 facts

Solution: Add constraints

# Fast: Matches specific events
KBS::Condition.new(:event, { kind: "error", severity: "critical" })
# Alpha memory: 50 facts

docs.title: 2. Expensive Predicates
docs.text:
Problem: Complex predicates evaluated repeatedly

# Slow: Expensive predicate called for every :data fact asserted
KBS::Condition.new(:data, { raw_data: ->(raw) { expensive_calculation(raw) } })

Solution: Pre-calculate

# Fast: Calculate once when adding fact
processed_value = expensive_calculation(raw_data)
engine.add_fact(:data, { processed: processed_value })

KBS::Condition.new(:data, { processed: :v? })

docs.title: 3. Action Overhead
docs.text:
Problem: Slow actions block engine

# Slow: Action makes API call
r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
  result = HTTParty.get("https://api.example.com/process")  # Blocks!
  engine.add_fact(:result, result)
end

Solution: Async processing

# Fast: Queue action, process asynchronously (KBS::Blackboard::Engine)
r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
  engine.post_message("rules", "api_queue", {
    url: "https://api.example.com/process",
    fact_id: facts[0].uuid
  }, priority: 50)
end

# Separate worker processes messages
worker = Thread.new do
  loop do
    msg = engine.consume_message("api_queue", "api_worker")
    break unless msg

    result = HTTParty.get(msg[:content][:url])
    # The engine is not thread-safe: hand the result back to the thread
    # that runs the engine (e.g. post it as another message) rather than
    # calling engine.add_fact from here
    engine.post_message("api_worker", "api_results", { body: result.body })
  end
end

docs.title: 4. Memory Leaks
docs.text:
Problem: Facts accumulate indefinitely

# Memory grows unbounded
loop do
  engine.add_fact(:sensor_reading, {
    value: read_sensor(),
    timestamp: Time.now
  })
  engine.run
end
# After 1 hour: 360,000 facts in memory!

Solution: Clean up old facts

A predicate is evaluated when the fact is asserted, so a rule cannot notice a reading becoming old later. Prune from the loop instead:

loop do
  engine.add_fact(:sensor_reading, {
    value: read_sensor(),
    timestamp: Time.now
  })
  engine.run

  cutoff = Time.now - 300  # 5 minutes
  engine.facts.each do |fact|
    engine.remove_fact(fact) if fact.type == :sensor_reading && fact[:timestamp] < cutoff
  end
end

Facts a rule asserts under logical conditions are retracted automatically when the facts that support them go.

docs.title: Rule Design
docs.text:
• Order conditions from most to least selective
  • Minimize negations (use positive logic where possible)
  • Keep predicates simple
  • Pre-calculate expensive values
  • Share patterns across rules

docs.title: Fact Management
docs.text:
• Remove facts when no longer needed
  • Batch fact additions
  • Use specific fact types (not generic :data)
  • Avoid duplicate facts (KBS::Engine.new(fact_duplication: false) makes add_fact return the existing equal fact)

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
• Keep actions fast
  • Avoid blocking I/O in actions
  • Use message passing for async work
  • Don't add/remove many facts in single action

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
• Choose backend based on requirements:
  • In-memory for speed
  • SQLite for persistence + moderate load
  • Redis for persistence + high load
  • Hybrid for production
  • Optimize SQLite with WAL mode and batch writes in transactions
  • Configure the Redis client you pass to RedisStore.new(redis:)
  • Monitor database size

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
• Profile before optimizing
  • Measure fact addition rate
  • Track engine run time
  • Monitor memory usage
  • Log rule firing frequency

docs.title: Performance Targets
docs.text: These are rough targets, not measurements, and the measured rates above differ from them substantially (in-memory assertion is much faster; a blackboard backend without batching is much slower). Use them as a starting point and measure your own workload.

docs.title: Expected Performance (In-Memory)
docs.text: Operation Target Notes Add fact 50,000/sec Simple facts, no rules Simple rule (1 condition) 10,000/sec Per fact Complex rule (3+ conditions) 1,000/sec Per fact Engine run (1000 facts, 10 rules) < 100ms Total time Negation check 10,000/sec Per token

docs.title: Expected Performance (SQLite)
docs.text: Operation Target Notes Add fact 5,000/sec With WAL mode Query facts 100,000/sec Indexed queries Transaction 1,000/sec Commit rate

docs.title: Expected Performance (Redis)
docs.text: Operation Target Notes Add fact 25,000/sec Network overhead Query facts 50,000/sec Hash operations Message queue 50,000/sec Sorted set operations

docs.title: Vertical Scaling
docs.text:
Increase single-process performance:

# 1. Use faster backend
store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(...)
engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(store: store)

# 2. Optimize rules
# - Order conditions
# - Minimize negations
# - Batch operations

# 3. Pre-process data
# - Calculate values before adding facts
# - Index frequently queried attributes

docs.title: Horizontal Scaling
docs.text:
Multiple processes sharing Redis:

Each engine matches only the facts asserted through it (plus the facts already in the store when its rules are added, which seed new alpha memories). Facts another process writes later do not reach its network, so hand work between processes through the shared message queue:

# Process 1: Data collector
collector_store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(
  url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0'
)
collector = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(store: collector_store)

# Collect data
loop do
  data = fetch_data()
  collector.post_message("collector", "raw_data", data)
end

# Process 2: Rule processor
processor_store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(
  url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0'  # Same Redis!
)
processor = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(store: processor_store)

# Add rules
processor.add_rule(...)

# Process data
loop do
  while (msg = processor.consume_message("raw_data", "processor"))
    processor.add_fact(:raw_data, msg[:content])
  end
  processor.run
  sleep 1
end

docs.title: Partitioning
docs.text:
Split facts by domain:

# Engine 1: Temperature monitoring
temp_engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'temp.db')
# Handles :temperature_reading, :hvac_control

# Engine 2: Security monitoring
security_engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'security.db')
# Handles :motion_sensor, :door_sensor, :alarm

# Coordinator: Coordinates between engines
coordinator_engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'coordinator.db')
# Handles cross-domain rules

docs.title: Testing Rules
docs.text: Comprehensive testing strategies for rule-based systems. This guide covers unit testing, integration testing, test fixtures, and coverage analysis for KBS applications.

docs.title: Testing Overview
docs.text:
Rule-based systems require testing at multiple levels:

  1. Unit Tests - Test individual rules in isolation
  2. Integration Tests - Test rule interactions
  3. Fact Fixtures - Reusable test data
  4. Coverage - Ensure all rules and conditions are tested
  5. Performance Tests - Verify rule execution speed

docs.title: Test Framework
docs.text:
# Gemfile
group :test do
  gem 'minitest', '~> 5.16'
  gem 'simplecov', require: false  # Coverage
  gem 'benchmark'                  # A bundled gem since Ruby 3.5; used by the performance tests
end

SimpleCov.start

require 'minitest/autorun'
require 'kbs'
require 'kbs/blackboard'  # Only needed for the blackboard persistence tests

class Minitest::Test
  def assert_rule_fired(kb, rule_name)
    # Check if rule action was executed
    # Implementation depends on tracking mechanism
  end

  def refute_rule_fired(kb, rule_name)
    # Check that rule did not fire

docs.title: Test Single Rule
docs.text:
A predicate such as greater_than(30) is the value of the attribute it tests; there is no separate predicate: key. A perform block runs with the rule builder as self, so a rule that asserts facts calls the knowledge base explicitly (kb.fact), and the test calls kb.run after kb is assigned.

require 'test_helper'

class TestTemperatureRule < Minitest::Test
  def build_kb(fired)
    kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
      rule "high_temp_alert", priority: 100 do
        on :sensor,
          type: "temperature",
          value: greater_than(30)

        perform do |facts, bindings|
          fired << true
          kb.fact :alert,
            type: "high_temperature",
            temperature: facts[0][:value]
        end
      end
    end
  end

  def test_fires_when_temperature_high
    fired = []
    kb = build_kb(fired)

    kb.fact :sensor, type: "temperature", value: 35
    kb.run

    assert fired.any?, "Rule should fire for high temperature"

    alerts = kb.engine.facts.select { |f| f.type == :alert }
    assert_equal 1, alerts.size
    assert_equal 35, alerts.first[:temperature]
  end

  def test_does_not_fire_when_temperature_normal
    fired = []
    kb = build_kb(fired)

    kb.fact :sensor, type: "temperature", value: 25
    kb.run

    assert_empty fired, "Rule should not fire for normal temperature"

    alerts = kb.engine.facts.select { |f| f.type == :alert }
    assert_empty alerts
  end

  def test_threshold_boundary
    fired = []
    kb = build_kb(fired)

    # Test at exact threshold
    kb.fact :sensor, type: "temperature", value: 30
    kb.run

    assert_empty fired, "Rule should not fire at exact threshold (> not >=)"
  end
end

      rule "high_temp_and_low_humidity" do
        on :temperature,
          location: :loc?,
          value: greater_than(30)

        on :humidity,
          location: :loc?,
          value: less_than(40)

          fired = true
        end
      end

      fact :humidity, location: "room1", value: 30

          location: :loc?,
          value: greater_than(30)

        on :humidity,
          location: :loc?,
          value: less_than(40)

        perform do |facts, bindings|
          fired = true
        end
      end

      fact :temperature, location: "room1", value: 35
      fact :humidity, location: "room2", value: 30
      run
    end

    refute fired, "Rule should not fire with different locations"
  end

  def test_does_not_fire_when_only_temperature_high

  end

    end

    refute fired, "Rule should not fire with normal temperature"
  end
end

class TestNegationRule < Minitest::Test
  def test_fires_when_error_not_acknowledged
    fired = false

    kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
      rule "alert_if_no_acknowledgment" do
        on :error, id: :id?
        without :acknowledged, error_id: :id?

        end
      end

      fact :error, id: 1
      run

  end

  def test_does_not_fire_when_error_acknowledged

    kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
      rule "alert_if_no_acknowledgment" do
        on :error, id: :id?
        without :acknowledged, error_id: :id?

        perform do |facts, bindings|
          fired = true
        end
      end

      fact :error, id: 1
      fact :acknowledged, error_id: 1
      run
    end

    refute fired, "Rule should not fire when error acknowledged"
  end
end

docs.title: Test Rule Interactions
docs.text:
class TestRuleInteractions < Minitest::Test
  def test_cascading_rules
    alerts = []

    kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
      # Rule 1: Detect high temperature
      rule "detect_high_temp" do
        on :sensor, value: greater_than(30)

        perform do |facts, bindings|
          kb.fact :temp_alert, severity: "high"
        end
      end

      # Rule 2: Escalate to critical
      rule "escalate_critical" do
        on :temp_alert, severity: "high"
        on :sensor, value: greater_than(40)

        perform do |facts, bindings|
          kb.fact :critical_alert, type: "temperature"
          alerts << :critical
        end
      end
    end

    # Add high temperature
    kb.fact :sensor, value: 45
    kb.run

    # Both rules fire: the alert asserted by the first rule activates the
    # second within the same run
    assert kb.engine.facts.any? { |f| f.type == :temp_alert }
    assert kb.engine.facts.any? { |f| f.type == :critical_alert }
    assert_includes alerts, :critical
  end

  def test_partial_cascade
    alerts = []

    kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
      rule "detect_high_temp" do
        on :sensor, value: greater_than(30)
        perform { kb.fact :temp_alert, severity: "high" }
      end

      rule "escalate_critical" do
        on :temp_alert, severity: "high"
        on :sensor, value: greater_than(40)
        perform do |facts, bindings|
          kb.fact :critical_alert, type: "temperature"
          alerts << :critical
        end
      end
    end

    # Add moderately high temperature
    kb.fact :sensor, value: 35
    kb.run

    # Only first rule fires
    assert kb.engine.facts.any? { |f| f.type == :temp_alert }
    refute kb.engine.facts.any? { |f| f.type == :critical_alert }
  end
end

docs.title: Track Rule Firings
docs.text:
class CoverageTracker
  def initialize(kb)
    @kb = kb
    @rule_firings = Hash.new(0)
  end

  def wrap_rules
    @kb.engine.rules.each do |rule|
      original_action = rule.action

      rule.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
        @rule_firings[rule.name] += 1
        original_action.call(facts, bindings)
      end
    end
  end

  def report
    puts "\n=== Coverage Report ==="

    total_rules = @kb.engine.rules.size
    fired_rules = @rule_firings.keys.size
    coverage = (fired_rules.to_f / total_rules * 100).round(2)

    puts "Rules: #{fired_rules}/#{total_rules} (#{coverage}%)"

    puts "\nRule Firings:"
    @rule_firings.each do |name, count|
      puts "  #{name}: #{count}"
    end

    untested = @kb.engine.rules.map(&:name) - @rule_firings.keys
    if untested.any?
      puts "\nUntested Rules:"
      untested.each { |name| puts "  - #{name}" }
    end
  end

  attr_reader :rule_firings
end

# Usage
class TestWithCoverage < Minitest::Test
  def test_coverage
    kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
      rule "rule1" do
        on :fact, {}
        perform { }
      end

      rule "rule2" do
        on :other, {}
        perform { }
      end
    end

    tracker = CoverageTracker.new(kb)
    tracker.wrap_rules

    # Add facts and run
    kb.fact :fact, {}
    kb.run

    tracker.report

    # Assert all rules fired
    # (or check specific coverage requirements)
  end
end

docs.text:
require 'benchmark'

class PerformanceTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_rule_performance
    time = Benchmark.measure do
      kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
        rule "perf_test" do
          on :data, value: :v?
          perform { }
        end

        # Add many facts
        1000.times { |i| fact :data, value: i }
        run
      end
    end

    assert time.real < 1.0, "Engine should complete in under 1 second"
  end

  def test_fact_addition_performance
    kb = KBS.knowledge_base

    time = Benchmark.measure do
      10_000.times { |i| kb.fact :data, value: i }
    end

    rate = 10_000 / time.real
    assert rate > 10_000, "Should add >10k facts/sec, got #{rate.round(2)}"
  end
end

class TestBlackboardPersistence < Minitest::Test
  def test_facts_persist_across_sessions
    # Session 1: Add facts
    engine1 = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'test.db')
    kb1 = KBS.knowledge_base(engine: engine1) do
      fact :sensor, id: 1, value: 25
    end
    kb1.close

    # Session 2: Load facts
    engine2 = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'test.db')
    assert_equal 1, engine2.facts.size
    assert_equal 25, engine2.facts.first[:value]

    engine2.close
    File.delete('test.db') if File.exist?('test.db')
  end

  def test_audit_trail
    engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: ':memory:')

    fact = engine.add_fact(:data, value: 1)
    engine.modify(fact, value: 2)
    engine.remove_fact(fact)

    # Newest entry first
    history = engine.blackboard.get_history(fact.uuid)

    assert_equal 3, history.size
    assert_equal %w[REMOVE UPDATE ADD], history.map { |entry| entry[:action] }

    engine.close
  end
end

def test_edge_cases
  # Empty facts
  kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
    rule "check" do
      on :sensor, value: :v?
      perform { }
    end
    run
  end
  assert_empty kb.engine.facts.select { |f| f.type == :alert }

  # Exact threshold
  kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
    rule "check" do
      on :sensor, value: greater_than(30)
      perform { }
    end
    fact :sensor, value: 30
  end
  assert_equal 0, kb.run  # run returns the number of rules fired

  # Just below threshold
  kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
    rule "check" do
      on :sensor, value: greater_than(30)
      perform { }
    end
    fact :sensor, value: 29.99
  end
  assert_equal 0, kb.run

  # Just above threshold
  kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
    rule "check" do
      on :sensor, value: greater_than(30)
      perform { }
    end
    fact :sensor, value: 30.01
  end
  assert_equal 1, kb.run
end
