docs.title: Negation
docs.text: Negated conditions match when a pattern is absent from working memory. This guide explains negation semantics, use cases, performance implications, and common pitfalls.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
KBS::Condition.new(:alert, { sensor_id: :id? }, negated: true)

Semantics: Condition satisfied when NO fact matches the pattern.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
KBS::Rule.new("send_first_alert") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    # Positive: High temperature detected
    KBS::Condition.new(:high_temp, { sensor_id: :id? }),

    # Negative: No alert sent yet
    KBS::Condition.new(:alert_sent, { sensor_id: :id? }, negated: true)
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    send_alert(bindings[:id?])
    engine.add_fact(:alert_sent, { sensor_id: bindings[:id?] })
  end
end

Behavior: - First run: :high_temp exists, :alert_sent doesn't → rule fires - Second run: Both :high_temp and :alert_sent exist → rule doesn't fire

docs.title: Open World Assumption
docs.text:
Negation means "no matching fact exists", not "fact is explicitly false":

# Negated condition
KBS::Condition.new(:error, { id: :id? }, negated: true)

# Matches when:
# - No :error fact exists with that id
# - Working memory is empty
# - :error facts exist but with different ids

# Does NOT match when:
# - Any :error fact with matching id exists

docs.title: Variable Binding in Negation
docs.text:
Variables in negated conditions still create join constraints:

r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: :id?, temp: :temp? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:alert, { sensor_id: :id? }, negated: true)
]

# For each sensor fact:
#   Check if NO alert exists with sensor_id == sensor's id
#   If no such alert: rule fires

docs.title: Negation Node Behavior
docs.text:
1. Token arrives with bindings { :id? => "bedroom" }
2. Look up :alert facts with sensor_id == "bedroom" (a hash lookup on the shared variable)
3. Link the token to each matching fact (its blockers)
4. If there are none: propagate token (condition satisfied)
5. If there are some: block token; it propagates when its last blocker is retracted

docs.title: 1. Guard Conditions
docs.text:
Prevent duplicate actions:

KBS::Rule.new("process_order") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:order, { id: :id?, status: "pending" }),
    KBS::Condition.new(:processing, { order_id: :id? }, negated: true)
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    # Only process if not already processing
    engine.add_fact(:processing, { order_id: bindings[:id?] })
    process_order(bindings[:id?])
  end
end

docs.title: 2. Missing Information Detection
docs.text:
Alert when expected data is absent:

KBS::Rule.new("missing_threshold") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: :id? }),
    KBS::Condition.new(:threshold, { sensor_id: :id? }, negated: true)
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    alert("Sensor #{bindings[:id?]} has no threshold configured!")
  end
end

docs.title: 3. State Transitions
docs.text:
Ensure prerequisites before transitioning:

KBS::Rule.new("activate_account") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:user, { id: :id?, email_verified: true }),
    KBS::Condition.new(:account_active, { user_id: :id? }, negated: true)
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    engine.add_fact(:account_active, { user_id: bindings[:id?] })
  end
end

docs.title: 4. Timeout Detection
docs.text:
Fire when response hasn't arrived:

KBS::Rule.new("timeout_alert") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:request, {
      id: :req_id?,
      created_at: ->(created) { (Time.now - created) > 300 }  # 5 minutes
    }),

    KBS::Condition.new(:response, { request_id: :req_id? }, negated: true)
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    alert("Request #{bindings[:req_id?]} timed out!")
  end
end

The created_at predicate is checked when the request is added, not as time passes, so a request has to be added (or modified) after it is already five minutes old to match.

docs.title: 5. Mutual Exclusion
docs.text:
Ensure only one option selected:

KBS::Rule.new("select_default") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:user, { id: :id? }),
    KBS::Condition.new(:preference, { user_id: :id?, theme: :theme? }, negated: true)
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    # No preference set → use default
    engine.add_fact(:preference, { user_id: bindings[:id?], theme: "light" })
  end
end

docs.title: Conjunction (AND)
docs.text:
All negations must be satisfied:

r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, {}),
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, {}, negated: true),
  KBS::Condition.new(:c, {}, negated: true)
]

# Fires when: a exists AND b doesn't exist AND c doesn't exist

docs.title: Complex Negation
docs.text:
KBS::Rule.new("unique_error") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:error, { type: :type? }),
    KBS::Condition.new(:error_handled, { type: :type? }, negated: true),
    KBS::Condition.new(:error_ignored, { type: :type? }, negated: true)
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    # Error exists but neither handled nor ignored
    handle_new_error(bindings[:type?])
  end
end

docs.title: Negation is Expensive
docs.text:
Reason: Must find the matching facts on every token arrival: a hash lookup when the negation shares a variable with an earlier condition, a scan of its alpha memory when it does not.

# Expensive: Large alpha memory to search
KBS::Condition.new(:log_entry, {}, negated: true)
# Must check all log_entry facts for each token

# Better: Specific pattern
KBS::Condition.new(:error_log, { severity: "critical" }, negated: true)
# Smaller alpha memory, fewer checks

docs.title: Negation Node Overhead
docs.text:
class NegationNode < QuantifierNode
  def left_activate(token)
    # For EVERY token: find the facts that block it (hash index on
    # shared variables, then any remaining tests) and link them
    matching_facts(token).each { |fact| link(token, fact) }

    emit(token) unless matched?(token)  # No blockers = condition satisfied
  end

  def right_deactivate(fact)
    # Follow the fact's links to the tokens it blocked; a token whose
    # last blocker is gone is passed on. No memory is searched.
  end
end

Cost: one lookup (or one alpha memory scan without a shared variable) per token; retracting a blocker only visits the tokens it blocked

docs.title: Optimization Strategies
docs.text:
1. Order negations last:

# Good: Positive conditions first
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, {}),
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, {}),
  KBS::Condition.new(:c, {}, negated: true)  # Last
]

# Bad: Negation first
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:c, {}, negated: true),  # First
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, {}),
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, {})
]

2. Minimize negations:

# Bad: Multiple negations
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:foo, {}, negated: true),
  KBS::Condition.new(:bar, {}, negated: true),
  KBS::Condition.new(:baz, {}, negated: true)
]

# Better: Single positive condition
# Add fact when conditions met:
unless foo_exists? || bar_exists? || baz_exists?
  engine.add_fact(:conditions_clear, {})
end

r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:conditions_clear, {})
]

3. Use specific patterns:

# Expensive
KBS::Condition.new(:event, {}, negated: true)

# Cheaper
KBS::Condition.new(:event, { type: "error", severity: "critical" }, negated: true)

docs.title: 1. Forgetting Variable Binding
docs.text:
# Bad: Variables don't connect
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: :id1? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:alert, { id: :id2? }, negated: true)  # Different variable!
]

# Good: Consistent variables
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: :id? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:alert, { sensor_id: :id? }, negated: true)  # Same :id?
]

docs.title: 2. Infinite Loops
docs.text:
An activation fires once, so a rule whose action changes nothing fires once per match and stops. It loops when the action changes a fact the rule matches, because the changed fact is a new match:

# Bad: Rule fires forever
KBS::Rule.new("infinite_loop") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:start, {}),
    KBS::Condition.new(:done, {}, negated: true)
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    # Modifying :start re-matches it; :done is never added!
    engine.modify(facts[0], count: facts[0][:count] + 1)
  end
end

# Good: Add termination fact
KBS::Rule.new("runs_once") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:start, {}),
    KBS::Condition.new(:done, {}, negated: true)
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    do_something()
    engine.add_fact(:done, {})  # Prevents re-firing
  end
end

docs.title: 3. Negation of Missing Attributes
docs.text:
# Doesn't work as expected: a missing key reads as nil, so any
# :sensor without an :error attribute blocks the rule
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { error: nil }, negated: true)

# Better: Check for absence of error fact
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: :id? }),
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor_error, { sensor_id: :id? }, negated: true)

docs.title: 4. Over-Using Negation
docs.text:
# Bad: Many negations
KBS::Rule.new("many_negations") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:a, {}, negated: true),
    KBS::Condition.new(:b, {}, negated: true),
    KBS::Condition.new(:c, {}, negated: true),
    KBS::Condition.new(:d, {}, negated: true)
  ]
  # Expensive! Checks 4 alpha memories per token
end

# Good: Refactor to positive logic
# Add a single fact representing "all clear" state

docs.title: Default Values
docs.text:
# If no preference, use default
KBS::Rule.new("set_default_theme") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:user, { id: :id? }),
    KBS::Condition.new(:theme_preference, { user_id: :id? }, negated: true)
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    engine.add_fact(:theme_preference, { user_id: bindings[:id?], theme: "dark" })
  end
end

docs.title: Cleanup Rules
docs.text:
# Remove orphaned records
KBS::Rule.new("cleanup_orphaned_comments") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:comment, { post_id: :pid? }),
    KBS::Condition.new(:post, { id: :pid? }, negated: true)
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    comment = facts[0]
    engine.remove_fact(comment)
  end
end

docs.title: Prerequisite Checking
docs.text:
# Ensure all prerequisites met
KBS::Rule.new("deploy_application") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:deploy_requested, {}),
    KBS::Condition.new(:tests_passed, {}),
    KBS::Condition.new(:build_succeeded, {}),
    KBS::Condition.new(:deployment_blocked, {}, negated: true)
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    deploy()
  end
end

docs.title: Trace Negation Checks
docs.text:
The engine builds its own KBS::NegationNodes, so trace them by prepending a module:

require 'debug_me'

module TraceNegation
  include DebugMe

  def left_activate(token)
    super
    debug_me { ['@alpha_memory.pattern', 'facts_matching(token).size', 'matched?(token) ? "BLOCK" : "PASS"'] }
  end
end

KBS::NegationNode.prepend(TraceNegation)

docs.title: Count Inhibitors
docs.text:
# Check how many facts are blocking tokens, per negated pattern
negations = engine.alpha_memories.each_value.flat_map(&:successors).grep(KBS::NegationNode).uniq

negations.to_h do |node|
  blockers = node.alpha_memory.items.count { |fact| node.tokens_matched_by(fact).any? }
  [node.alpha_memory.pattern, blockers]
end
# => {{sensor_id: :id?, type: :alert} => 1}

docs.title: Validate Negation Logic
docs.text:
# Test: Rule should fire when condition absent
engine.add_fact(:trigger, {})
engine.run
assert rule_fired, "Should fire when negated condition absent"

# Test: Rule should NOT fire when condition present
engine.add_fact(:blocker, {})
engine.run
refute rule_fired, "Should not fire when negated condition present"

docs.title: The Opposite Test: exists
docs.text:
without matches while no fact fits a pattern. exists matches while at least one does, and matches once however many there are:

rule "unpaid orders remain" do
  on :order, id: :id?
  without :payment, order_id: :id?   # no payment for this order
  exists :customer_service, open: true  # and somebody is on duty
  perform { |facts, bindings| escalate(bindings[:id?]) }
end

Neither kind of condition adds a fact to the match, and a variable first used in one is not bound for later conditions. Both are kept up to date by links between each partial match and the facts that satisfy it, so adding or retracting a fact only visits the matches it affects.

With the low-level API, pass exists: true or negated: true to KBS::Condition.new.

docs.title: Alternatives to Negation
docs.text: Sometimes positive logic is clearer and faster:

docs.title: Pattern: Explicit State
docs.text:
# Instead of:
KBS::Condition.new(:processing, { id: :id? }, negated: true)

# Use explicit state:
KBS::Condition.new(:status, { id: :id?, value: "idle" })

docs.title: Pattern: Status Flags
docs.text:
# Instead of:
KBS::Condition.new(:error, {}, negated: true)

# Use status flag:
KBS::Condition.new(:system_status, { healthy: true })

docs.title: Pattern: Computed Facts
docs.text:
# Instead of checking absence in rule:
KBS::Condition.new(:response, { req_id: :id? }, negated: true)

# Add a fact when timeout occurs:
KBS::Rule.new("detect_timeout") do |r|
  r.conditions = [
    KBS::Condition.new(:request, {
      id: :id?,
      created_at: ->(time) { (Time.now - time) > 300 }
    })
  ]

  r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
    engine.add_fact(:timeout, { request_id: bindings[:id?] })
  end
end

# Then use positive check:
KBS::Condition.new(:timeout, { request_id: :id? })

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Pattern Matching - How negation fits with pattern matching
  • Variable Binding - Variables in negated conditions
  • Network Structure - Negation node implementation
  • Performance Guide - Optimizing negation performance

Negation is powerful but expensive. Use sparingly and order last for best performance.

docs.title: Pattern Matching
docs.text: Deep dive into KBS pattern matching semantics. Learn how the RETE algorithm matches facts against condition patterns efficiently.

docs.title: Matching Fundamentals
docs.text:
Pattern matching determines whether a fact satisfies a condition. A match occurs when:

  1. Type matches - Fact type equals condition type
  2. Attributes match - Every pattern value is satisfied: a literal must be equal, a ?variable accepts any value, and a predicate (a lambda) must return truthy
  3. Join tests pass - A variable already bound by an earlier condition must have the same value
# Condition pattern
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, {
  id: "bedroom",
  temp: :temp?
})

# Matching fact
fact = { type: :sensor, id: "bedroom", temp: 28 }
# ✓ Type: :sensor == :sensor
# ✓ Attribute id: "bedroom" == "bedroom"
# ✓ Attribute temp: :temp? binds to 28
# MATCH!

# Non-matching fact
fact = { type: :sensor, id: "kitchen", temp: 28 }
# ✓ Type: :sensor == :sensor
# ✗ Attribute id: "kitchen" != "bedroom"
# NO MATCH

docs.title: Type Matching
docs.text:
Facts match only when types are identical:

# Condition
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, {})

# Matches
engine.add_fact(:stock, { symbol: "AAPL" })  # ✓

# Does not match
engine.add_fact(:stocks, { symbol: "AAPL" })  # ✗ (:stocks != :stock)
engine.add_fact("stock", { symbol: "AAPL" })  # ✗ (String != Symbol)

Type comparison uses ==, so symbols and strings never match.

docs.title: Exact Equality
docs.text:
# Match exact value
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: "bedroom" })

# Matches
{ type: :sensor, id: "bedroom" }  # ✓

# Does not match
{ type: :sensor, id: "kitchen" }   # ✗
{ type: :sensor, id: :bedroom }     # ✗ (Symbol != String)

docs.title: Multiple Literals
docs.text:
# All must match
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, {
  symbol: "AAPL",
  exchange: "NASDAQ"
})

# Matches
{ type: :stock, symbol: "AAPL", exchange: "NASDAQ" }  # ✓

# Does not match
{ type: :stock, symbol: "AAPL", exchange: "NYSE" }    # ✗
{ type: :stock, symbol: "GOOGL", exchange: "NASDAQ" } # ✗

docs.title: Nil Values
docs.text:
# Match nil explicitly
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { error: nil })

# Matches
{ type: :sensor, error: nil }  # ✓
{ type: :sensor }              # ✓ (a missing key reads as nil)

# Does not match
{ type: :sensor, error: false }  # ✗ (false != nil)

docs.title: Basic Binding
docs.text:
Variables end with ? and bind to fact attribute values:

# Condition with variable
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { temp: :t? })

# Matching fact
fact = { type: :sensor, temp: 28 }

# After matching:
bindings = { :t? => 28 }

A variable accepts any value, so it also matches a fact that lacks the attribute; the variable is then bound to nil.

docs.title: Multiple Bindings
docs.text:
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, {
  symbol: :sym?,
  price: :p?,
  volume: :v?
})

# Fact
{ type: :stock, symbol: "AAPL", price: 150, volume: 1000 }

# Bindings
{
  :sym? => "AAPL",
  :p? => 150,
  :v? => 1000
}

docs.title: Mixed Literals and Variables
docs.text:
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, {
  id: "bedroom",     # Literal (must equal "bedroom")
  temp: :temp?       # Variable (binds to any value)
})

# Matches only bedroom sensor, binds temp
{ type: :sensor, id: "bedroom", temp: 28 }  # ✓ binds :temp? => 28
{ type: :sensor, id: "kitchen", temp: 28 }  # ✗ id doesn't match

docs.title: Cross-Condition Binding
docs.text:
Variables create join constraints across conditions:

r.conditions = [
  # Condition 1: Binds :sym?
  KBS::Condition.new(:stock, { symbol: :sym?, price: :price? }),

  # Condition 2: Tests :sym? (must be same value)
  KBS::Condition.new(:watchlist, { symbol: :sym? })
]

# Facts
stock1 = { type: :stock, symbol: "AAPL", price: 150 }
stock2 = { type: :stock, symbol: "GOOGL", price: 2800 }
watchlist = { type: :watchlist, symbol: "AAPL" }

# Matches
# stock1 + watchlist: ✓ (:sym? = "AAPL" in both)

# Does not match
# stock2 + watchlist: ✗ (:sym? = "GOOGL" in stock, "AAPL" in watchlist)

docs.title: Binding Semantics
docs.text:
1. First occurrence binds - Variable's first use establishes the value
  2. Subsequent uses test - Later uses check equality
  3. Scope is per-rule - Variables don't cross rules
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, { x: :v? }),  # Binds :v?
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, { y: :v? }),  # Tests :v? (must equal)
  KBS::Condition.new(:c, { z: :v? })   # Tests :v? (must equal)
]

# All three facts must have same value for x, y, z

docs.title: Match Any
docs.text:
Empty pattern {} matches all facts of that type:

# Matches ALL sensor facts
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, {})

# Matches these
{ type: :sensor, id: "bedroom", temp: 28 }
{ type: :sensor, id: "kitchen", temp: 22 }
{ type: :sensor, foo: "bar", baz: 123 }

docs.title: Selectivity Warning
docs.text:
Empty patterns have minimal selectivity:

# Bad: Very unselective (matches thousands)
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:log_entry, {}),     # Matches 10,000 facts
  KBS::Condition.new(:error, { id: 1 })   # Matches 1 fact
]
# Creates 10,000 partial matches!

# Good: Specific first
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:error, { id: 1 }),    # Matches 1 fact
  KBS::Condition.new(:log_entry, {})        # Joins with 10,000
]
# Creates 1 partial match

docs.title: Custom Predicates
docs.text: Predicates add complex matching beyond equality. A predicate is a lambda given as the value of the attribute it tests; there is no separate predicate: option. The lambda is called with that attribute's value:

docs.title: Basic Predicate
docs.text:
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, { price: ->(price) { price > 100 } })

# Matches
{ type: :stock, price: 150 }  # ✓ (150 > 100)

# Does not match
{ type: :stock, price: 50 }   # ✗ (50 <= 100)
{ type: :stock }              # ✗ (a predicate is not called for a nil value)

In the DSL, helpers such as greater_than(100), between(20, 30) and one_of(...) build these lambdas for you.

docs.title: Predicate Evaluation
docs.text:
A fact is checked against each entry of the pattern:

  1. Type check
  2. Each attribute: literal equality, ?variable (always passes), or predicate call
  3. Join tests on variables bound by earlier conditions (in the beta network)
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: "bedroom", temp: ->(t) { t.between?(20, 30) } })

# Evaluation:
# 1. type == :sensor? ✓
# 2. id == "bedroom"? ✓
# 3. temp.between?(20, 30)? ✓
# MATCH!

A predicate sees one attribute value and runs when the fact is added (or modified), not again later.

docs.title: Predicate Limitations
docs.text:
Predicates limit network sharing:

# Rule 1
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, { price: ->(p) { p > 100 } })

# Rule 2 (different predicate)
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, { price: ->(p) { p < 50 } })

# These create SEPARATE alpha memories
# Cannot share pattern matching computation

Alpha memories are keyed by pattern, and two lambda objects are never equal, so even identical-looking predicates in two rules get two memories. Reuse the same lambda object to share one.

Use pattern matching when possible:

# Bad: Predicate for simple equality
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, { symbol: ->(s) { s == "AAPL" } })

# Good: Pattern matching
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, { symbol: "AAPL" })

docs.title: Conjunctive Matching (AND)
docs.text:
All conditions must match:

r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, {}),
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, {}),
  KBS::Condition.new(:c, {})
]

# Rule fires when:
# a_fact exists AND b_fact exists AND c_fact exists

docs.title: Disjunctive Matching (OR)
docs.text:
Use multiple rules:

# Fire when A OR B
rule1 = KBS::Rule.new("fire_on_a") do |r|
  r.conditions = [KBS::Condition.new(:a, {})]
  r.action = lambda { |f, b| common_action }
end

rule2 = KBS::Rule.new("fire_on_b") do |r|
  r.conditions = [KBS::Condition.new(:b, {})]
  r.action = lambda { |f, b| common_action }
end

Or use predicates:

KBS::Condition.new(:event, { kind: ->(k) { k == "a" || k == "b" } })

docs.title: Negation (NOT)
docs.text:
Match when pattern is absent:

r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, {}),
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, {}, negated: true)  # NOT B
]

# Fires when: a_fact exists AND no b_fact exists

See Negation Guide for details.

docs.title: Range Checks
docs.text:
# Temperature in range 20-30
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { temp: ->(t) { t.between?(20, 30) } })

docs.title: String Matching
docs.text:
# Symbol starts with "TECH"
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, { symbol: ->(sym) { sym.start_with?("TECH") } })

# Regex match
KBS::Condition.new(:log, { message: ->(msg) { msg =~ /ERROR|FATAL/ } })

docs.title: Collection Membership
docs.text:
# Status is one of pending, processing, approved
KBS::Condition.new(:order, {
  status: ->(status) { %w[pending processing approved].include?(status) }
})

docs.title: Temporal Conditions
docs.text:
# Reading older than 5 minutes
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { timestamp: ->(time) { (Time.now - time) > 300 } })

The predicate is evaluated when the fact is added. A reading that is fresh then does not start matching five minutes later; modify the fact or assert a clock fact to have it checked again.

docs.title: Computed Values
docs.text:
A predicate sees only its own attribute, so a test that needs several attributes of the same fact works best on a value computed when the fact is added:

# Price changed more than 10%
change = (current_price - previous_price).abs / previous_price.to_f
engine.add_fact(:stock, symbol: "AAPL", current_price: current_price,
                        previous_price: previous_price, change: change)

KBS::Condition.new(:stock, { symbol: :sym?, change: ->(c) { c > 0.10 } })

docs.title: Nested Attribute Access
docs.text:
# Access nested hash
KBS::Condition.new(:event, {
  data: ->(data) { data.is_a?(Hash) && data[:severity] == "critical" }
})

docs.title: Alpha Network
docs.text:
Facts are tested against patterns in alpha memory:

# Pattern
{ type: :stock, symbol: "AAPL" }

# Alpha memories are grouped by fact type, and a pattern with a
# literal is filed under its first literal (symbol: "AAPL"), so a
# new fact reaches it with one hash lookup on its own value.
# Only matching facts are stored in alpha memory.

docs.title: Join Network
docs.text:
Partial matches combine in beta network:

r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, {}),  # 100 matches
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, {})   # 200 matches
]

# No shared variables: 100 × 200 = 20,000 combinations
# With a shared ?variable, join memories are hash-indexed on it,
# so each token only meets the facts with the same value

docs.title: Optimization Strategies
docs.text:
1. Specific patterns first:

# Good
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:critical, {}),  # 1 match
  KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, {})     # 1000 matches
]
# Beta memory size: 1

# Bad
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, {}),     # 1000 matches
  KBS::Condition.new(:critical, {})    # 1 match
]
# Beta memory size: 1000

2. Use literals over predicates:

# Good: O(1) hash lookup
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, { exchange: "NASDAQ" })

# Bad: predicate called for every :stock fact
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, { exchange: ->(e) { e == "NASDAQ" } })

3. Minimize empty patterns:

# Expensive
KBS::Condition.new(:log_entry, {})  # Matches everything

# Better
KBS::Condition.new(:log_entry, { level: "ERROR" })  # More selective

docs.title: Trace Matching
docs.text:
Fact#matches? takes a pattern hash (the condition's pattern plus its :type) and tells you whether a fact fits:

pattern = { type: :sensor, id: "bedroom" }

engine.facts.map { |fact| [fact.attributes, fact.matches?(pattern)] }
# => [[{id: "bedroom", temp: 28}, true], [{id: "kitchen", temp: 22}, false]]

docs.title: Inspect Alpha Memories
docs.text:
engine.alpha_memories.each do |pattern, memory|
  puts "Pattern: #{pattern}"
  puts "  Matches: #{memory.items.size}"
  memory.items.each do |fact|
    puts "    #{fact.attributes}"
  end
end

docs.title: Test Patterns in Isolation
docs.text:
condition = KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { temp: ->(t) { t > 30 } })

fact = KBS::Fact.new(:sensor, { temp: 35 })

# Manually test
fact.matches?(condition.pattern.merge(type: condition.type))  # => true

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Variable Binding - Join tests and binding extraction
  • Negation - Negated condition behavior
  • RETE Algorithm - How matching works internally
  • Performance Guide - Optimization techniques

Pattern matching is the heart of the RETE algorithm. Efficient patterns = fast rule systems.

docs.title: Persistence Options
docs.text: KBS offers multiple storage backends for persistent facts. This guide helps you choose and configure the right storage for your use case.

docs.title: 1. No Persistence (Default)
docs.text:
Transient in-memory facts using KBS::Engine:

engine = KBS::Engine.new

# Facts exist only in memory
engine.add_fact(:sensor, { temp: 28 })

# Lost on exit

When to use: - Prototyping - Short-lived processes - Pure computation (no state retention needed) - Testing

Pros: - ✅ Fastest (no I/O) - ✅ Zero configuration - ✅ Simple

Cons: - ❌ No persistence - ❌ Lost on crash - ❌ No audit trail

docs.title: 2. SQLite (Default Persistent)
docs.text:
Embedded database using KBS::Blackboard::Engine:

require 'kbs/blackboard'  # not loaded by require 'kbs'

engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'kb.db')

engine.add_fact(:sensor, { temp: 28 })
engine.close

# Next run
engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'kb.db')
puts engine.facts.size  # => 1 (persisted)

When to use: - Single-process applications - Moderate fact volumes (< 1M facts) - ACID transaction requirements - Complete audit trails - No external dependencies

Pros: - ✅ Embedded (no server) - ✅ ACID guarantees - ✅ Durable - ✅ Full audit trail - ✅ SQL queries available (engine.blackboard.query_facts(sql, params))

Cons: - ❌ Slower than Redis - ❌ Single writer - ❌ Not distributed

Configuration:

engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(
  db_path: 'kb.db'           # Database file path (default ':memory:')
)

# WAL mode for better concurrency, set on the SQLite3::Database
engine.blackboard.store.db.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")

docs.title: 3. Redis (High Performance)
docs.text:
In-memory data structure store:

require 'kbs/blackboard'  # the Redis stores also need the redis gem

store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(
  url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0'
)

engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(store: store)

With a Redis store the message queue and audit log are kept in Redis too.

When to use: - High-frequency updates (> 1000 writes/sec) - Real-time systems (trading, IoT) - Distributed systems (multiple engines) - Large fact volumes - Speed is critical

Pros: - ✅ Faster than SQLite for high write rates - ✅ Distributed (multiple engines share data) - ✅ Perfect for real-time - ✅ Scalable

Cons: - ❌ Requires Redis server - ❌ Volatile by default (enable RDB/AOF for persistence) - ❌ No ACID across keys - ❌ Audit trail capped (latest 1,000 entries per fact or rule, 10,000 overall) and no SQL queries

Configuration:

store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(
  url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0',  # Ignored when redis: is given
  session_id: nil,                  # Defaults to a new UUID
  redis: nil                        # An existing Redis client to use
)

Retracted facts stay in Redis until engine.blackboard.vacuum removes those retracted more than 30 days ago.

Redis Persistence Options:

# In redis.conf:

# RDB: Point-in-time snapshots
save 900 1      # Save after 900s if 1 key changed
save 300 10     # Save after 300s if 10 keys changed

# AOF: Append-only file (durability)
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec  # Sync to disk every second

docs.title: 4. Hybrid (Best of Both)
docs.text:
Combines Redis (speed) with SQLite (durability):

require 'kbs/blackboard'

store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::HybridStore.new(
  redis_url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0',
  db_path: 'audit.db'
)

engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(store: store)

How it works: - Facts: Stored in Redis (fast access) - Audit log: Written to SQLite (durable history) - Messages: Redis sorted sets (fast priority queue)

When to use: - Production systems requiring both speed and auditing - Regulatory compliance (need audit trail) - High-frequency updates with history requirements - Distributed systems needing accountability

Pros: - ✅ Fast fact access (Redis) - ✅ Durable audit trail (SQLite) - ✅ Best of both worlds - ✅ Can reconstruct from audit log

Cons: - ❌ Requires both Redis and SQLite - ❌ More complex setup - ❌ Slightly slower writes (each change also writes the SQLite audit log) - ❌ No transactions (Redis and SQLite writes are separate)

Configuration:

store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::HybridStore.new(
  redis_url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0',  # Ignored when redis: is given
  redis: nil,                              # An existing Redis client
  db_path: 'audit.db',                     # SQLite audit log (the default)
  session_id: nil                          # Defaults to a new UUID
)

Fact changes and rule firings are always logged to SQLite.

docs.title: Decision Tree
docs.text:
Need persistence?
├─ No → KBS::Engine (default)
└─ Yes
   │
   ├─ Need speed > 1000 ops/sec?
   │  ├─ Yes
   │  │  ├─ Need audit trail?
   │  │  │  ├─ Yes → Hybrid Store
   │  │  │  └─ No → Redis Store
   │  │  └─ No → Redis Store
   │  │
   │  └─ No
   │     ├─ Need distributed access?
   │     │  └─ Yes → Redis Store
   │     └─ No → SQLite Store
   │
   └─ Single machine, moderate load?
      └─ SQLite Store

docs.title: By Use Case
docs.text:
IoT / Real-Time Sensors: 

# High frequency, need speed
store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(
  url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0'
)

Trading Systems: 

# Speed + audit trail for compliance
store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::HybridStore.new(
  redis_url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0',
  db_path: 'trading_audit.db'
)

Expert Systems: 

# Moderate load, need durability
engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'expert.db')

Development / Testing: 

# No persistence needed
engine = KBS::Engine.new

docs.title: SQLite → Redis
docs.text:
# 1. Load from SQLite
sqlite_engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'old.db')
facts = sqlite_engine.facts

# 2. Save to Redis
redis_store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(
  url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0'
)
redis_engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(store: redis_store)

facts.each do |fact|
  redis_engine.add_fact(fact.type, fact.attributes)
end

docs.title: Redis → SQLite
docs.text:
# 1. Load from Redis
redis_store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(
  url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0'
)
redis_engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(store: redis_store)
facts = redis_engine.facts

# 2. Save to SQLite
sqlite_engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'new.db')

facts.each do |fact|
  sqlite_engine.add_fact(fact.type, fact.attributes)
end

sqlite_engine.close

docs.title: Write Performance
docs.text:
require 'benchmark'

# SQLite
sqlite_engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'perf.db')
Benchmark.bm do |x|
  x.report("SQLite writes:") do
    10_000.times { |i| sqlite_engine.add_fact(:test, { value: i }) }
  end
end

# Redis
redis_store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(
  url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0'
)
redis_engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(store: redis_store)
Benchmark.bm do |x|
  x.report("Redis writes:") do
    10_000.times { |i| redis_engine.add_fact(:test, { value: i }) }
  end
end

docs.title: Read Performance
docs.text:
# SQLite
Benchmark.bm do |x|
  x.report("SQLite reads:") do
    100.times { sqlite_engine.facts }
  end
end

# Redis
Benchmark.bm do |x|
  x.report("Redis reads:") do
    100.times { redis_engine.facts }
  end
end

Results depend on your hardware, Redis setup and SQLite pragmas; run these against your own workload. engine.facts reads every active fact from the store each time, so it slows as the store grows.

docs.title: Custom Persistence
docs.text:
Implement your own backend by subclassing KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::Store. A store keeps facts only; the blackboard picks its message queue and audit log by what the store offers, so it must also respond to db (a SQLite3 database) or connection (a Redis client):

class PostgresStore < KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::Store
  attr_reader :session_id

  def add_fact(uuid, type, attributes)
    # Insert into PostgreSQL
  end

  def remove_fact(uuid)
    # Mark retracted; return { type:, attributes: }, or nil if not found
  end

  def update_fact(uuid, attributes)
    # Replace attributes; return the fact's type, or nil
  end

  def get_fact(uuid)
    # Return { uuid:, type:, attributes: }, or nil
  end

  def get_facts(type = nil, pattern = {})
    # Return an Array of { uuid:, type:, attributes: } for active facts
  end

  def transaction
    yield
  end

  # Also: query_facts, register_knowledge_source, clear_session,
  # stats, vacuum, close

  def connection
    # A Redis client for the message queue and audit log
  end
end

# Use custom store
store = PostgresStore.new(connection_string: "...")
engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(store: store)

See Custom Persistence for details.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
# Enable WAL mode for better concurrency
engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'kb.db')
db = engine.blackboard.store.db

db.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")
db.execute("PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL")  # Trade some durability for speed
db.execute("PRAGMA cache_size = -64000")   # 64MB cache

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
# Configure the client yourself and pass it in
client = Redis.new(url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0', timeout: 5)

store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(redis: client)

docs.title: Hybrid
docs.text: The hybrid store writes each audit record to SQLite as the change happens; there is no batching to configure.

docs.title: SQLite Database Locked
docs.text:
# Increase busy timeout
engine = KBS::Blackboard::Engine.new(db_path: 'kb.db')
engine.blackboard.store.db.busy_timeout = 5000  # Wait up to 5 seconds

docs.title: Redis Connection Issues
docs.text:
# Enable retry logic on the client
client = Redis.new(
  url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0',
  reconnect_attempts: 3
)

store = KBS::Blackboard::Persistence::RedisStore.new(redis: client)

docs.text:
• Blackboard Memory - Using persistent blackboard
  • Custom Persistence - Implementing custom stores
  • Performance Guide - Optimizing storage performance
  • API Reference - Complete blackboard API

Choose your backend based on speed, durability, and distribution requirements.

docs.title: Truth Maintenance
docs.text:
A rule often asserts a fact that is only true while the rule's conditions hold: a sensor above 90 degrees is overheating, an order with no payment is overdue. Without help, such a derived fact stays in working memory after the reason for it is gone, and you write a second rule to clean it up.

Mark the conditions as logical and the engine does the cleanup. A fact asserted by the rule is then supported by the match of those conditions. When the match goes away, the fact is retracted.

docs.title: A First Example
docs.text:
kb = KBS.knowledge_base

kb.rule "overheating" do
  logical do
    on :sensor, id: :id?, temp: greater_than(90)
  end
  perform { |_facts, bindings| kb.assert(:overheating, sensor: bindings[:id?]) }
end

reading = kb.assert(:sensor, id: 1, temp: 95)
kb.run
kb.facts.map(&:type)   # => [:sensor, :overheating]

kb.modify(reading, temp: 60)
kb.facts.map(&:type)   # => [:sensor]

The :overheating fact was never retracted by a rule. It went because the sensor no longer matched.

A match stops when one of its facts is retracted, when modify changes a fact so it no longer fits, or when a fact arrives that a without condition in the block forbids.

docs.title: What the Support Covers
docs.text:
Only the conditions inside logical do ... end carry the support, and the block has to come before the rule's other conditions:

rule "page the operator" do
  logical do
    on :overheating, sensor: :id?
  end
  on :shift_change            # a trigger, not a reason
  perform { |_f, b| kb.assert(:page, sensor: b[:id?]) }
end

Retracting :shift_change leaves the :page alone. Retracting :overheating removes it.

A logical condition after a plain one raises ArgumentError when the rule is added.

without and exists work inside the block:

rule "overdue" do
  logical do
    on :order, id: :id?
    without :payment, order_id: :id?
  end
  perform { |_f, b| kb.assert(:overdue, order: b[:id?]) }
end

Asserting the payment retracts :overdue.

docs.title: Chains
docs.text:
A derived fact can support others. Retracting the first fact unwinds the whole chain:

rule "overheating" do
  logical { on :sensor, temp: greater_than(90) }
  perform { kb.assert(:overheating) }
end

rule "alarm" do
  logical { on :overheating }
  perform { kb.assert(:alarm) }
end

Retract the sensor and both :overheating and :alarm go.

docs.title: Unconditional Facts
docs.text:
A fact is supported only when a rule with logical conditions asserts it. Facts you assert yourself, and facts asserted by rules without a logical block, are unconditional: they stay until something retracts them.

When the engine rejects duplicate facts (fact_duplication: false), the same fact can be asserted more than once, and the two kinds of support combine:

A supported fact is asserted again... Result by another logical match it gains a second support, and goes when both are gone from outside a logical rule it becomes unconditional

An unconditional fact asserted again by a logical rule stays unconditional.

With duplication on, which is the default, each assertion makes a separate fact with its own single support.

docs.title: Looking at the Support
docs.text:
engine.logically_supported?(fact)  # true while the fact depends on a match
engine.dependencies(fact)          # the matches that support it, as arrays of facts
engine.dependents(fact)            # the facts that have this fact in a supporting match

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Unsupported facts are retracted as soon as the change that removed their support has been matched, before the next rule fires.
  • Retracting a supported fact yourself is fine; its support is forgotten.
  • If a rule's action removes its own support and then asserts a fact, that fact is not added and add_fact returns nil.
  • A rule whose action asserts the very fact its logical without forbids retracts that fact at once, matches again, and fires again. Bound it with run(limit) or restructure the rule.
  • Supports live in the engine's memory. With a persistent blackboard, derived facts are stored like any other fact, but the links to their supports are not saved.

docs.title: With the Low-Level API
docs.text:
KBS::Rule.new(
  "overheating",
  conditions: [KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { temp: ->(t) { t > 90 } }, logical: true)],
  action: ->(_facts) { engine.add_fact(:overheating, {}) }
)

docs.title: Variable Binding
docs.text: Variables connect facts across conditions, enabling join constraints in the RETE network. This guide explains how binding works, join tests, and optimization strategies.

docs.title: Variable Syntax
docs.text:
Variables end with ? and are symbols:

:temp?      # Variable named "temp"
:sensor_id? # Variable named "sensor_id"
:x?         # Variable named "x"

Naming conventions: - Use lowercase with underscores - Be descriptive - Match domain terminology

docs.title: Single Variable
docs.text:
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { temp: :t? })

# Matches fact:
{ type: :sensor, temp: 28 }

# Creates binding:
{ :t? => 28 }

docs.title: Multiple Variables
docs.text:
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, {
  symbol: :sym?,
  price: :price?,
  volume: :vol?
})

# Matches:
{ type: :stock, symbol: "AAPL", price: 150, volume: 1000 }

# Bindings:
{
  :sym? => "AAPL",
  :price? => 150,
  :vol? => 1000
}

docs.title: Join Constraints
docs.text:
Variables with the same name create equality constraints:

r.conditions = [
  # Condition 1: Binds :id? to sensor's id
  KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: :id?, temp: :temp? }),

  # Condition 2: Must match same :id?
  KBS::Condition.new(:threshold, { sensor_id: :id?, max: :max? })
]

Join test: 

sensor[:id] == threshold[:sensor_id]

docs.title: Multiple Joins
docs.text:
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, { x: :v1?, y: :v2? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, { p: :v1?, q: :v3? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:c, { m: :v2?, n: :v3? })
]

# Join tests:
# a[:x] == b[:p]  (via :v1?)
# a[:y] == c[:m]  (via :v2?)
# b[:q] == c[:n]  (via :v3?)

docs.title: Visual Example
docs.text:
Condition 1: stock(symbol: :sym?, price: :p?)
Condition 2: watchlist(symbol: :sym?)
Condition 3: alert_config(symbol: :sym?, threshold: :t?)

Variable :sym? creates two joins:
├─ stock[:symbol] == watchlist[:symbol]
└─ stock[:symbol] == alert_config[:symbol]

docs.title: 1. First Occurrence: Bind
docs.text:
# First condition with :sym?
KBS::Condition.new(:stock, { symbol: :sym? })

# Fact matches
{ type: :stock, symbol: "AAPL" }

# Binding created:
{ :sym? => "AAPL" }

docs.title: 2. Subsequent Occurrences: Test
docs.text:
# Second condition with :sym?
KBS::Condition.new(:watchlist, { symbol: :sym? })

# Checks if symbol == "AAPL" (from previous binding)
# Matches:
{ type: :watchlist, symbol: "AAPL" }  # ✓

# Does not match:
{ type: :watchlist, symbol: "GOOGL" }  # ✗

Scope rules: - A variable used twice in one condition compares two attributes of the same fact: { min: :v?, max: :v? } matches only when min == max. - A variable that first appears in a negated (without) or exists condition is local to that condition. Such conditions add no fact to the match, so they bind nothing for later conditions or for the action.

docs.title: 3. Action: Access
docs.text:
r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
  # Access bound variables
  symbol = bindings[:sym?]
  price = bindings[:p?]

  puts "#{symbol} at $#{price}"
end

docs.title: What is a Join Test?
docs.text:
A join test verifies that variable values match across facts:

r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, { x: :v? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, { y: :v? })
]

# Join test structure:
{
  token_field_index: 0,     # Index of fact in token (first condition)
  token_field: :x,          # Attribute name in first fact
  fact_field: :y,           # Attribute name in new fact
  operation: :eq            # Equality test
}

docs.title: Join Test Execution
docs.text:
A simplified version of KBS::JoinTests#join_test_passes?:

def perform_join_test(token, new_fact, test)
  # Get value from token (previous facts)
  token_fact = token.fact_at(test[:token_field_index])
  token_value = token_fact[test[:token_field]]

  # Get value from new fact
  fact_value = new_fact[test[:fact_field]]

  # Test equality
  token_value == fact_value
end

docs.title: Example Execution
docs.text:
# Rule
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: :id?, temp: :temp? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:threshold, { sensor_id: :id?, max: :max? })
]

# Facts
sensor = { type: :sensor, id: "bedroom", temp: 28 }
threshold = { type: :threshold, sensor_id: "bedroom", max: 25 }

# Join execution:
# 1. sensor matches → token created
token = KBS::Token.new(root_token, sensor, join_node)
# Bindings: { :id? => "bedroom", :temp? => 28 }

# 2. threshold tested against token
test = {
  token_field_index: 0,       # sensor is first fact
  token_field: :id,           # sensor's id attribute
  fact_field: :sensor_id,     # threshold's sensor_id attribute
  operation: :eq
}

# 3. Perform join
token_value = sensor[:id]              # "bedroom"
fact_value = threshold[:sensor_id]     # "bedroom"
result = token_value == fact_value     # true
# ✓ Join succeeds → new token created

docs.title: Pattern 1: Primary Key Join
docs.text:
Connect facts via identifier:

r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:order, {
    id: :order_id?,
    status: "pending"
  }),

  KBS::Condition.new(:payment, {
    order_id: :order_id?,
    verified: true
  })
]

# Matches orders with verified payments

docs.title: Pattern 2: Multi-Attribute Join
docs.text:
Join on multiple fields:

r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:trade, {
    symbol: :sym?,
    date: :date?,
    volume: :vol?
  }),

  KBS::Condition.new(:settlement, {
    symbol: :sym?,
    trade_date: :date?
  })
]

# Joins on both symbol AND date

docs.title: Pattern 3: Transitive Binding
docs.text:
Chain bindings across three+ conditions:

r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, { id: :x? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, { a_id: :x?, id: :y? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:c, { b_id: :y? })
]

# a[:id] == b[:a_id]
# b[:id] == c[:b_id]
# Creates chain: a → b → c

docs.title: Pattern 4: Fan-Out Join
docs.text:
One fact joins with multiple:

r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: :id?, temp: :t? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:threshold, { sensor_id: :id? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:alert_config, { sensor_id: :id? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:location, { sensor_id: :id? })
]

# All join on :id?

docs.title: Join Cardinality
docs.text:
# Condition 1: 100 sensor facts
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { temp: :t? })

# Condition 2: 200 threshold facts
KBS::Condition.new(:threshold, { max: :m? })

# Without variable binding:
# Potential matches: 100 × 200 = 20,000

# With variable binding:
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: :id?, temp: :t? })
KBS::Condition.new(:threshold, { sensor_id: :id?, max: :m? })

# Actual matches: ~100 (1:1 relationship)

Variable bindings dramatically reduce join size.

docs.title: Beta Memory Size
docs.text:
# Bad: No shared variables
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, {}),  # 1000 facts
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, {}),  # 1000 facts
  KBS::Condition.new(:c, {})   # 1000 facts
]
# Beta memory: 1000 × 1000 × 1000 = 1,000,000,000 tokens!

# Good: Shared variables
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, { id: :id? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, { a_id: :id? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:c, { a_id: :id? })
]
# Beta memory: ~1000 tokens (assuming 1:1:1 relationship)

docs.title: Optimization Tips
docs.text:
1. Use specific bindings:

# Good: Binds sensor to specific readings
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: :id? })
KBS::Condition.new(:reading, { sensor_id: :id? })

# Bad: No binding (cross product)
KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, {})
KBS::Condition.new(:reading, {})

2. Order by selectivity:

# Good: Specific first
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:critical_alert, { id: :id? }),  # 1 fact
  KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: :id? })          # 1000 facts
]
# Beta memory: 1 token

# Bad: General first
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:sensor, { id: :id? }),          # 1000 facts
  KBS::Condition.new(:critical_alert, { id: :id? })   # 1 fact
]
# Beta memory: 1000 tokens

3. Minimize cross products:

# Bad: No shared variables between first two conditions
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, { x: :v1? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, { y: :v2? }),  # No :v1?!
  KBS::Condition.new(:c, { p: :v1?, q: :v2? })
]
# Creates a × b cross product

# Good: Progressive joining
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:a, { x: :v1? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:c, { p: :v1?, q: :v2? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:b, { y: :v2? })
]
# Each condition reduces search space

docs.title: One-to-Many Relationship
docs.text:
# One customer, many orders
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:customer, {
    id: :cust_id?,
    status: "active"
  }),

  KBS::Condition.new(:order, {
    customer_id: :cust_id?,
    status: "pending"
  })
]

# Fires once per pending order for active customers

docs.title: Many-to-Many Relationship
docs.text:
# Students enrolled in courses
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:student, { id: :student_id? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:enrollment, {
    student_id: :student_id?,
    course_id: :course_id?
  }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:course, { id: :course_id? })
]

# Fires for each student-course pair

docs.title: Hierarchical Join
docs.text:
# Parent → Child → Grandchild
r.conditions = [
  KBS::Condition.new(:category, { id: :cat_id? }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:product, {
    category_id: :cat_id?,
    id: :prod_id?
  }),
  KBS::Condition.new(:review, {
    product_id: :prod_id?,
    rating: :rating?
  })
]

docs.title: Print Bindings
docs.text:
r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
  puts "Bindings: #{bindings.inspect}"
  puts "Facts:"
  facts.each_with_index do |fact, i|
    puts "  #{i}: #{fact.type} #{fact.attributes}"
  end
end

docs.title: Inspect Join Tests
docs.text:
KBS::JoinTestBuilder compiles a rule's conditions into the join tests the network uses, one array per condition:

KBS::JoinTestBuilder.new(rule.conditions).tests
# => [[], [{token_field_index: 0, token_field: :id, fact_field: :sensor_id, operation: :eq}]]

Equality tests between a token field and a fact field become hash-index keys on the join node's memories, so they are looked up rather than evaluated per candidate.

docs.title: Validate Bindings
docs.text:
r.action = lambda do |facts, bindings|
  # Ensure expected bindings exist
  required = [:sensor_id?, :temp?, :max?]
  missing = required - bindings.keys

  if missing.any?
    raise "Missing bindings: #{missing}"
  end

  # Proceed with action
  # ...
end

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Pattern Matching - How facts match conditions
  • Negation - Negated conditions and binding
  • Network Structure - How joins compile into networks
  • Performance Guide - Optimizing join performance

Variable binding is the glue that connects facts. Master bindings, master rule performance.

docs.title: Writing Rules
docs.text: Master the art of authoring production rules. This guide covers best practices, patterns, and strategies for writing effective, maintainable, and performant rules in KBS.

docs.title: Rule Anatomy
docs.text:
Every rule consists of three parts:

KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "rule_name", priority: 0 do
    # 1. CONDITIONS - Pattern matching
    on :fact_type, attr: value

    # 2. ACTION - What to do when conditions match
    perform do |facts, bindings|
      # Execute logic
    end
  end
end

docs.title: 1. Rule Name
docs.text:
Choose descriptive, actionable names:

# Good: Clear intent
"send_high_temperature_alert"
"cancel_duplicate_orders"
"escalate_critical_issues"

# Bad: Vague or cryptic
"rule1"
"process"
"check_stuff"

Naming Conventions: - Use snake_case - Start with verb (action-oriented) - Be specific about what the rule does - Include domain context

docs.title: 2. Priority
docs.text:
Control execution order when multiple rules match:

KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "critical_safety_check", priority: 100 do  # Fires first
    # ...
  end

  rule "normal_processing", priority: 50 do
    # ...
  end

  rule "cleanup_task", priority: 10 do            # Fires last
    # ...
  end
end

Priority Guidelines: - 100+ - Safety checks, emergency shutdowns - 50-99 - Business logic, processing - 1-49 - Monitoring, logging, cleanup - 0 - Default priority (no preference)

docs.title: 3. Conditions
docs.text:
Patterns that must match for the rule to fire. Order matters for performance.

KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "example" do
    # Most selective first (fewest matches)
    on :critical_alert, severity: "critical"

    # Less selective last (more matches)
    on :sensor, id: :sensor_id?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      # Action
    end
  end
end

docs.title: 4. Action
docs.text:
Code executed when all conditions match:

KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "example" do
    on :alert, message: :msg?
    on :sensor, id: :sensor_id?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      # Access matched facts
      alert = facts[0]
      sensor = facts[1]

      # Access variable bindings
      sensor_id = bindings[:sensor_id?]

      # Perform action
      notify_operator(sensor_id, alert[:message])
    end
  end
end

facts holds one fact per positive condition, in order; without and exists conditions contribute none. bindings maps each ?variable to its value.

Working memory inside perform: the action block runs with the rule builder as self. Once the rule is built, the builder forwards fact, assert, retract, modify, query, facts, halt and engine to the knowledge base, so bare calls work. Condition keywords (on, without, exists, logical, perform and their aliases) raise KBS::RuleBuiltError there, since they can no longer change the rule. Calling the knowledge base through a local works as well:

kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "derive" do
    on :sensor, temp: :temp?
    perform do |facts, bindings|
      kb.fact :reading_seen, temp: bindings[:temp?]
    end
  end
end

kb.fact :sensor, temp: 28
kb.run   # call run after `kb` is assigned

The examples below use either form.

docs.title: Condition Ordering
docs.text: Golden Rule: Order conditions from most selective to least selective.

docs.title: Why Order Matters
docs.text:
# Bad: General condition first
KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "inefficient" do
    on :sensor, {}           # 1000 matches
    on :critical_alert, {}   # 1 match
    perform { }
  end
end
# Creates 1000 partial matches, wastes memory

# Good: Specific condition first
KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "efficient" do
    on :critical_alert, {}   # 1 match
    on :sensor, {}           # Joins with 1000
    perform { }
  end
end
# Creates 1 partial match, efficient joins

docs.title: Selectivity Examples
docs.text:
# Most selective (few facts)
on :emergency, level: "critical"
on :user, role: "admin"

# Moderate selectivity
on :order, status: "pending"
on :stock, exchange: "NYSE"

# Least selective (many facts)
on :sensor, {}
on :log_entry, {}

docs.title: Measuring Selectivity
docs.text:
def measure_selectivity(kb, type, pattern)
  kb.engine.facts.count { |f|
    f.type == type &&
    pattern.all? { |k, v| f[k] == v }
  }
end

# Compare
puts measure_selectivity(kb, :critical_alert, {})  # => 1
puts measure_selectivity(kb, :sensor, {})          # => 1000

# Order: critical_alert first, sensor second

docs.title: Single Responsibility
docs.text:
One action, one purpose:

# Good: Focused action
KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "send_email" do
    on :alert, email: :email?, message: :message?
    perform do |facts, bindings|
      send_email_alert(bindings[:email?], bindings[:message?])
    end
  end
end

# Bad: Multiple responsibilities
KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "do_everything" do
    on :trigger, email: :email?, id: :id?, data: :data?, msg: :msg?
    perform do |facts, bindings|
      send_email_alert(bindings[:email?])
      update_database(bindings[:id?])
      call_external_api(bindings[:data?])
      write_log_file(bindings[:msg?])
    end
  end
end

Split complex actions into multiple rules:

kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  # Rule 1: Detect condition
  rule "detect_high_temp", priority: 50 do
    on :sensor, temp: greater_than(30)

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      kb.fact :high_temp_detected, temp: facts[0][:temp]
    end
  end

  # Rule 2: Send alert
  rule "send_temp_alert", priority: 40 do
    on :high_temp_detected, temp: :temp?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      send_email("High temp: #{bindings[:temp?]}")
    end
  end

  # Rule 3: Log event
  rule "log_temp_event", priority: 30 do
    on :high_temp_detected, temp: :temp?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      logger.info("Temperature spike: #{bindings[:temp?]}")
    end
  end
end

docs.title: Avoid Side Effects
docs.text:
Actions should be deterministic and idempotent when possible:

# Good: Idempotent (safe to run multiple times)
kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "update_alert" do
    on :trigger, id: :id?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      # Remove old alert if exists
      old = kb.query(:alert, id: bindings[:id?]).first
      kb.retract(old) if old

      # Add new alert
      kb.fact :alert, id: bindings[:id?], message: "Alert!"
    end
  end
end

# Bad: Non-idempotent (creates duplicates)
kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "duplicate_alerts" do
    on :trigger, id: :id?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      # Always adds, even if alert already exists
      kb.fact :alert, id: bindings[:id?], message: "Alert!"
    end
  end
end

Alternatively, turn duplicate facts off with kb.engine.fact_duplication = false (or KBS::Engine.new(fact_duplication: false)): asserting a fact equal to one already in working memory then returns the existing fact instead of adding another.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Protect against failures:

kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "safe_email" do
    on :alert, email: :email?, message: :message?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      begin
        send_email(bindings[:email?], bindings[:message?])
      rescue Net::SMTPError => e
        logger.error("Failed to send email: #{e.message}")
        # Add failure fact for retry logic
        kb.fact :email_failure,
          email: bindings[:email?],
          error: e.message,
          timestamp: Time.now
      end
    end
  end
end

docs.title: Consistent Naming
docs.text:
Use descriptive, consistent variable names:

# Good: Clear intent
:sensor_id?
:temperature_celsius?
:alert_threshold?
:user_email?

# Bad: Cryptic
:s?
:t?
:x?

docs.title: Join Patterns
docs.text:
Connect facts through shared variables:

KBS.knowledge_base do
  # Pattern: Join sensor reading with threshold
  rule "check_threshold" do
    on :sensor,
      id: :sensor_id?,
      temp: :current_temp?

    on :threshold,
      sensor_id: :sensor_id?,  # Same variable = join constraint
      max_temp: :max_temp?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      # Only matches when sensor_id is same in both facts
    end
  end
end

docs.title: Computed Bindings
docs.text:
Derive values in actions:

KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "calculate_diff" do
    on :sensor, temp: :current_temp?
    on :threshold, max_temp: :max_temp?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      current = bindings[:current_temp?]
      max = bindings[:max_temp?]

      # Compute derived values
      diff = current - max
      percentage_over = ((current / max.to_f) - 1) * 100

      puts "#{diff}°C over threshold (#{percentage_over.round(1)}%)"
    end
  end
end

docs.title: State Machine
docs.text:
Model state transitions:

kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  # Transition: pending → processing
  rule "start_processing" do
    on :order,
      id: :order_id?,
      status: "pending"

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      kb.modify(facts[0], status: "processing", started_at: Time.now)
    end
  end

  # Transition: processing → completed
  rule "complete_processing" do
    on :order,
      id: :order_id?,
      status: "processing"
    on :processing_done,
      order_id: :order_id?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      kb.retract(facts[1])  # Remove trigger
      kb.modify(facts[0], status: "completed", completed_at: Time.now)
    end
  end
end

kb.modify changes a fact's attributes and matches it again, as a retraction followed by an assertion, so the next transition rule can match it. Assigning order[:status] = ... does not re-match the fact.

docs.title: Guard Conditions
docs.text:
Prevent duplicate actions:

kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "send_alert_once" do
    on :high_temp, sensor_id: :id?

    # Guard: Only fire if alert not already sent
    without :alert_sent, sensor_id: :id?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      send_alert(bindings[:id?])

      # Record that we sent this alert
      kb.fact :alert_sent, sensor_id: bindings[:id?]
    end
  end
end

docs.title: Cleanup Rules
docs.text:
Remove stale facts:

kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "cleanup_stale_alerts", priority: 1 do
    on :alert,
      timestamp: ->(t) { (Time.now - t) > 3600 }  # 1 hour old

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      kb.retract(facts[0])
      logger.info("Removed stale alert")
    end
  end
end

A predicate is tested when the fact is asserted or modified, not again as time passes. To re-check an aging fact, re-match it with kb.modify(alert, {}) (or assert a fresh tick fact your rules depend on).

docs.title: Aggregation Rules
docs.text:
Compute over multiple facts:

kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "compute_average_temp" do
    on :compute_avg_requested, {}

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      temps = kb.query(:sensor)
        .map { |f| f[:temp] }
        .compact

      avg = temps.sum / temps.size.to_f

      kb.fact :average_temp, value: avg
    end
  end
end

docs.title: Temporal Rules
docs.text:
React to time-based conditions:

KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "detect_delayed_response" do
    on :request,
      id: :req_id?,
      created_at: ->(t) { (Time.now - t) > 300 }  # 5 minutes

    without :response,
      request_id: :req_id?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      alert("Request #{bindings[:req_id?]} delayed!")
    end
  end
end

As with the cleanup rule, the age test runs when the request is asserted or modified; re-match pending requests periodically with kb.modify(request, {}).

docs.title: Priority Levels
docs.text:
Establish consistent priority levels for your domain:

# Define priority constants
module Priority
  CRITICAL = 100   # Emergency, safety
  HIGH = 75        # Important business logic
  NORMAL = 50      # Standard processing
  LOW = 25         # Cleanup, logging
  MONITORING = 10  # Metrics, diagnostics
end

# Use in rules
KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "emergency_shutdown", priority: Priority::CRITICAL do
    # ...
  end

  rule "process_order", priority: Priority::NORMAL do
    # ...
  end
end

docs.title: Priority Inversion
docs.text:
Priority only orders the activations that are on the agenda at the same time. run keeps firing until the agenda is empty, so a high-priority rule that depends on a fact produced by a low-priority rule still fires in the same run, but only after the low-priority rule, and after every activation that outranks it:

# Risky: emergency_check waits for compute_risk (priority 10), so any
# priority 11-99 activation fires before the emergency check can
kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "compute_risk", priority: 10 do
    on :data, value: :v?
    perform do |facts, bindings|
      kb.fact :risk_score, value: calculate_risk(bindings[:v?])
    end
  end

  rule "emergency_check", priority: 100 do
    on :risk_score, value: :risk?  # Depends on low priority rule!
    perform do |facts, bindings|
      emergency_shutdown if bindings[:risk?] > 90
    end
  end
end

# Fix: Make dependency higher priority
kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "compute_risk", priority: 110 do  # Now runs before other work
    on :data, value: :v?
    perform do |facts, bindings|
      kb.fact :risk_score, value: calculate_risk(bindings[:v?])
    end
  end

  rule "emergency_check", priority: 100 do
    on :risk_score, value: :risk?
    perform do |facts, bindings|
      emergency_shutdown if bindings[:risk?] > 90
    end
  end
end

docs.title: Unit Test Rules in Isolation
docs.text:
require 'minitest/autorun'
require 'kbs'

class TestTemperatureRules < Minitest::Test
  def test_fires_when_temp_exceeds_threshold
    alert_fired = false

    kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
      rule "high_temp_alert" do
        on :sensor, id: :id?, temp: :temp?
        on :threshold, id: :id?, max: :max?

        perform do |facts, bindings|
          alert_fired = true if bindings[:temp?] > bindings[:max?]
        end
      end

      fact :sensor, id: "bedroom", temp: 30
      fact :threshold, id: "bedroom", max: 25
      run
    end

    assert alert_fired, "Rule should fire when temp > threshold"
  end

  def test_does_not_fire_when_temp_below_threshold
    alert_fired = false

    kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
      rule "high_temp_alert" do
        on :sensor, id: :id?, temp: :temp?
        on :threshold, id: :id?, max: :max?

        perform do |facts, bindings|
          alert_fired = true if bindings[:temp?] > bindings[:max?]
        end
      end

      fact :sensor, id: "bedroom", temp: 20
      fact :threshold, id: "bedroom", max: 25
      run
    end

    refute alert_fired, "Rule should not fire when temp <= threshold"
  end

  def test_only_fires_for_matching_sensor
    alert_fired = false

    kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
      rule "high_temp_alert" do
        on :sensor, id: :id?, temp: :temp?
        on :threshold, id: :id?, max: :max?

        perform do |facts, bindings|
          alert_fired = true if bindings[:temp?] > bindings[:max?]
        end
      end

      fact :sensor, id: "bedroom", temp: 30
      fact :threshold, id: "kitchen", max: 25
      run
    end

    refute alert_fired, "Rule should not fire for different sensors"
  end
end

docs.title: Integration Tests
docs.text:
Test multiple rules working together:

def test_state_machine_workflow
  kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
    # Add state transition rules
    rule "start_processing" do
      on :order, id: :id?, status: "pending"
      perform do |facts, bindings|
        kb.retract(facts[0])
        kb.fact :order, id: bindings[:id?], status: "processing"
      end
    end

    rule "complete_processing" do
      on :order, id: :id?, status: "processing"
      on :processing_done, order_id: :id?
      perform do |facts, bindings|
        kb.retract(facts[0])
        kb.retract(facts[1])
        kb.fact :order, id: bindings[:id?], status: "completed"
      end
    end

    # Add initial state
    fact :order, id: 1, status: "pending"
  end
  kb.run

  # Started, but not completed yet
  order = kb.engine.facts.find { |f| f.type == :order && f[:id] == 1 }
  assert_equal "processing", order[:status]

  # Trigger transition
  kb.fact :processing_done, order_id: 1
  kb.run

  # Should transition to completed
  order = kb.engine.facts.find { |f| f.type == :order && f[:id] == 1 }
  assert_equal "completed", order[:status]
end

docs.title: Property-Based Testing
docs.text:
Test rule invariants:

def test_no_duplicate_alerts
  kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
    rule "send_alert_once" do
      on :high_temp, sensor_id: :id?
      without :alert_sent, sensor_id: :id?

      perform do |facts, bindings|
        send_alert(bindings[:id?])
        kb.fact :alert_sent, sensor_id: bindings[:id?]
      end
    end

    # Add facts
    100.times do |i|
      fact :high_temp, sensor_id: i
    end
  end

  # Run engine multiple times
  10.times { kb.run }

  # Property: At most one alert per sensor
  alert_counts = kb.engine.facts
    .select { |f| f.type == :alert_sent }
    .group_by { |f| f[:sensor_id] }
    .transform_values(&:count)

  alert_counts.each do |sensor_id, count|
    assert_equal 1, count, "Sensor #{sensor_id} has #{count} alerts, expected 1"
  end
end

docs.title: Minimize Negations
docs.text:
Each negation adds a node to the rule's path that tracks, for every partial match, the facts that block it. Negations that share a ?variable with earlier conditions are hash-indexed; unconstrained ones (like without :foo, {}) are checked against every partial match:

# Expensive: 3 negations
KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "many_negations" do
    without :foo, {}
    without :bar, {}
    without :baz, {}
    perform { }
  end
end

# Better: Combine into positive condition
KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "positive_logic" do
    on :conditions_met, {}
    perform { }
  end

  # Add conditions_met fact if foo, bar, baz don't exist
  unless engine.facts.any? { |f| [:foo, :bar, :baz].include?(f.type) }
    fact :conditions_met, {}
  end
end

docs.title: Avoid Predicates for Simple Checks
docs.text:
A constant test is filed in a hash, so a fact reaches the matching alpha memory with one lookup on its value, and rules with the same pattern share that memory. A lambda is called for every fact of the type, and two patterns share a memory only when they hold the same lambda object.

# Expensive: Lambda called for every :stock fact
KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "with_predicate" do
    on :stock, symbol: ->(s) { s == "AAPL" }
    perform { }
  end
end

# Better: Use pattern matching
KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "with_pattern" do
    on :stock, symbol: "AAPL"
    perform { }
  end
end

docs.title: Cache Computed Values
docs.text:
# Bad: Recomputes every time rule fires
kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "check_average" do
    on :sensor, temp: :temp?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      avg = compute_expensive_average(kb.facts)
      alert(avg) if avg > threshold
    end
  end
end

# Good: Cache as fact, recompute only when needed
kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "update_average", priority: 100 do
    on :sensor, temp: :temp?  # Triggers when sensor added

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      avg = compute_expensive_average(kb.facts)
      kb.fact :cached_average, value: avg
    end
  end

  rule "check_average", priority: 50 do
    on :cached_average, value: :avg?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      alert(bindings[:avg?]) if bindings[:avg?] > threshold
    end
  end
end

docs.title: 1. Infinite Loops
docs.text:
# Bad: Rule fires itself indefinitely
kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "infinite_loop" do
    on :sensor, temp: :temp?

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      # This triggers the rule again!
      kb.fact :sensor, temp: bindings[:temp?] + 1
    end
  end
end

# Fix: Add termination condition
kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "limited_increment" do
    on :sensor, temp: :temp?
    without :increment_done, {}

    perform do |facts, bindings|
      kb.fact :sensor, temp: bindings[:temp?] + 1
      kb.fact :increment_done, {}
    end
  end
end

As a safety net while developing, kb.run(100) stops after 100 firings, and kb.halt called from an action stops the current run.

docs.title: 2. Writing Conditions Inside perform
docs.text:
# Bad: the rule is already built when the action runs
kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "derive" do
    on :reading, {}
    perform { on :other }   # raises KBS::RuleBuiltError during run
  end
end

# Fine: working-memory calls, bare or through kb
kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "derive" do
    on :reading, {}
    perform { fact :derived, {} }   # same as kb.fact :derived, {}
  end
end

docs.title: 3. Forgetting to Call run
docs.text:
Facts are matched as they are added, but matching only puts activations on the agenda; rules fire when run is called.

# Bad: Facts matched but rules never fire
kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "example" do
    on :sensor, temp: :temp?
    on :threshold, max: :max?
    perform { }
  end

  fact :sensor, temp: 30
  fact :threshold, max: 25
  # Rules never fire!
end

# Good: Run after adding facts
kb = KBS.knowledge_base do
  rule "example" do
    on :sensor, temp: :temp?
    on :threshold, max: :max?
    perform { }
  end

  fact :sensor, temp: 30
  fact :threshold, max: 25
  run  # Match and fire rules
end
